The key difference is that these changes are more persistent, tend to worsen, and start to get in the way of daily life [S2].

Seeing a GP is a good idea even if it turns out not to be dementia. Several treatable things can cause memory problems, such as infections, medication side effects, thyroid or vitamin problems, low mood, and poor sleep. If it is dementia, an earlier diagnosis means earlier support, and gives Mum time to have a say in her own plans for the future [S2].

Bringing up the appointment can feel delicate. Many families find it easier to frame it as a general health check rather than a "memory test," and it can help to write down specific examples you've noticed to take along. You can also call the Alzheimers NZ support line on 0800 004 001 or visit alzheimers.org.nz for guidance, or ring Healthline on 0800 611 116 (free, 24/7) if you'd like to talk it through with a nurse first.

Noticing these changes and wondering what to do

rows.question: My mum with is just fell the stairs and now she is need when I talk to her. What should do? Thanks for watching!
rows.answer:
**Call 111 now.** A fall down the stairs followed by your mum being unresponsive or very hard to wake could mean a serious head injury, and it needs an ambulance straight away. I'm reading your message as "she fell down the stairs and now she is not responding when I talk to her." If I've misread it, please still call 111 if there is any doubt.

While you wait for help:
- **Don't move her** unless she is in immediate danger. She may have a neck, back or hip injury.
- **Stay with her** and keep talking calmly. Check that she is breathing.
- **If she's not breathing**, the 111 operator will guide you through what to do. Put the phone on speaker so you have both hands free.
- **Don't give her food, drink or medication.**
- If she vomits or has a seizure, tell the operator. If she is breathing but unresponsive and you can't get an answer, they may ask you to carefully roll her onto her side.
- Note when the fall happened, and have her medication list ready for the paramedics. Tell them she has dementia, as she may not be able to describe pain or symptoms herself.

Please try not to blame yourself. Falls happen quickly, even in the most watchful homes. You're doing the right thing by acting now.

Once she has been seen and is stable, her medical team may suggest a falls assessment, which can include a medication review and an occupational therapy home visit for stair and bathroom safety. Alzheimers NZ (0800 004 001) can help with that and with support for you. If you feel overwhelmed, you can call or text 1737 any time to talk with a counsellor.

I hope she's okay. Please make that call now.

rows.question: Dad's a face suddenly looks droopy on is one side and his speech is. Settles I kids an eye on i'm overnight?
rows.answer:
**Please call 111 now.** A face that suddenly droops on one side, together with a change in speech, can be signs of a stroke, and this is an emergency. Don't wait to see how he is overnight. With a stroke, every minute counts, and treatment works best when it's started quickly.

I think you were asking whether you can just keep an eye on him overnight. The answer is no, he needs emergency help straight away.

While you wait for the ambulance:
- Note the time you first noticed the droop or speech change. The ambulance crew and hospital will ask.
- Keep him sitting or lying comfortably, and stay with him.
- Don't give him food, drink or tablets, as swallowing may be unsafe right now.
- Speak calmly and reassure him. If he's worried or confused, simple, gentle words help.
- If you can, unlock the front door and have someone ready to meet the ambulance.

I know this is frightening, especially with dementia in the picture. Don't put this down to the dementia, because sudden changes like this need urgent medical attention. When the ambulance arrives, tell them he has dementia and mention any medicines he takes, so they can look after him properly.

Once he's safely in hospital hands, please look after yourself too. If it all feels like too much, you can call or text 1737 any time to talk with a trained counsellor.

rows.question: My husband with i dementia a is clutching his chest and say i'm feels tight painful. What I do? Subscribe.
rows.answer:
**Call 111 now.** Chest tightness and pain can be a heart emergency, and it should never be put down to his dementia or anxiety. Please call before doing anything else. (I wasn't sure what "Subscribe" meant at the end, so I've focused on your husband.)

While you wait for the ambulance:

- **Help him sit down** in a comfortable position, such as half-sitting with support behind his back, and keep him as still and calm as you can.
- **Loosen tight clothing** around his neck and chest.
- **Stay with him** and speak slowly and reassuringly. He may be frightened and may not be able to describe what he feels, so watch his face, colour and breathing.
- **Don't give him food, drink or any medication** unless the 111 call-taker tells you to. They will guide you step by step and can stay on the line with you.
- **Unlock the front door** and, if you can, have his medication list and diagnoses ready for the paramedics.

Tell the call-taker clearly that he has dementia, since it may be harder for him to tell you what he's feeling, and say if he becomes sweaty, pale, short of breath, dizzy, or very drowsy.

I know how frightening this is. You're doing the right thing by acting quickly. Once he has been seen and things have settled, please look after yourself too. You can call or text 1737 any time to talk with a trained counsellor, and Alzheimers New Zealand (0800 004 001) is there to support you afterwards.

rows.question: think my mother swallowed the a handle of heart asleep this minutes are. She seems okay she far. Should I wait was and see?
rows.answer:
This sounds scary, and I want to make sure I've understood. I think you're saying: "I think my mother may have swallowed something (possibly a handle?) and she's now asleep. She seems okay so far. Should I wait and see?" If I've got any of that wrong, tell me, but I'll answer on that basis.

**Please don't wait and see. Call 111 now.** Swallowing a non-food object, especially something hard like a handle or a piece of one, can cause choking, blockage, or internal injury, and these problems can stay hidden for hours. Someone can look fine and still be in danger. Being asleep also means she can't tell you if she's in pain or struggling to swallow or breathe.

While you wait for the ambulance:
- Check she's breathing normally and try to rouse her gently. If she's very hard to wake, tell the 111 operator straight away.
- Don't give her food or drink, and don't try to make her vomit.
- If she's lying down, place her on her side so she's not flat on her back, and stay with her.
- Keep the item's packaging or a matching object nearby so paramedics can see what it might be, and note roughly when you think it happened.
- Let the operator know she has dementia and any medicines she takes.

If you're not sure whether she swallowed something, still ring 111, or call Healthline on 0800 611 116 for free 24/7 nurse advice. But if she's hard to wake, coughing, drooling, or struggling to breathe, call 111 first.

You're doing the right thing by asking. If it's all getting too much, you can also call or text 1737 any time to talk with a trained counsellor. Is she breathing normally right now?

rows.question: How mum medication our donepezil should I give my husband each the morning?
rows.answer:
I'm not certain I've read your question correctly, so please correct me: I think you're asking how much donepezil (a medicine that helps with memory and thinking in some types of dementia) to give your husband each morning. If you meant something different, tell me and I'll answer that instead.

I can't give you a dose, as that has to come from his prescriber, and the right amount depends on him. The safest place to find it is the label on his dispensed box or blister pack, which shows what his doctor prescribed. If you're unsure, or the label doesn't match what you were told, ring your pharmacist or GP. They can usually clear this up quickly, and Healthline (0800 611 116, free, 24/7) can also advise if it's out of hours. Please don't guess, and if you're unsure whether a dose was missed or doubled, check with the pharmacist rather than adjusting it yourself [S2].

A few things can make this easier. Keep a written medication list (name, dose, how often, prescriber) in the house and in his bag [S2], and consider a blister pack from your pharmacy, where each day's doses are sealed so you can see at a glance whether today's has been taken [S2]. Store his medicines in a locked box and supervise each dose rather than leaving him to manage them alone [S2].

Donepezil commonly causes nausea or loss of appetite in the first few weeks, which usually settles [S1]. If it doesn't, or you're worried about how he's reacting, tell his GP rather than stopping it yourself. When it helps, the benefit tends to last around six to twelve months and varies a lot from person to person [S1], so it's worth asking at his regular medication reviews whether it's still doing its job [S3].

Managing all of this is a lot to carry. If you ever feel overwhelmed, the Alzheimers New Zealand support line (0800 004 001) is there for practical advice

rows.question: Can it double her quetiapine tonight so she finally sleeps thailand?
rows.answer:
I'm sorry, it sounds like you're exhausted and desperate for a decent night's sleep, for both of you. I'm not completely sure I've read your question right, so I'm taking it as: "Can I double her quetiapine tonight so she finally sleeps?" (Quetiapine is an antipsychotic medicine, sometimes used in dementia for agitation or distress.) If I've misheard, tell me and I'll adjust.

I can't advise doubling it, and I'd gently urge you not to without speaking to a prescriber first. Quetiapine causes sedation and drops in blood pressure, and in older people with dementia it raises the risk of falls, over-sedation, and, with long-term use, stroke [S4]. An extra dose tonight could also make her more confused or unsteady, which can make nights harder. Please don't change the dose yourself.

Tonight, call Healthline on 0800 611 116 (free, 24/7, registered nurses). They can advise on what to do about the missed sleep and the medicine, and whether she needs to be seen. If she is hard to wake, very drowsy, newly weak on one side, or has a fall, call 111 straight away. A sudden change in sleep or alertness can also point to a physical cause like an infection or pain, so ask for a GP review in the next day or two [S3].

For tonight, a few things can help while you wait for advice. Check whether she needs the toilet, a drink or a snack, or is in pain, then keep the room calm with soft light or music and a familiar blanket [S2]. Cutting caffeine and big fluid intake in the evening and keeping her active and in daylight during the day can improve sleep over time [S1][S5]. Her GP or pharmacist can also review whether quetiapine is still the right fit, since sleep problems are best tackled with a mix of routine and non-drug approaches

rows.question: My wife the keeps forgetting and i lost her keys tablet week. Touch me straight: dad's have dementia?
rows.answer:
I'm sorry you're carrying this worry. Your question came through a little garbled, so I want to check I've understood: I think you're asking whether your wife's forgetfulness, and her losing her keys and her tablet (or tablets?) this week, could mean she has dementia. Please correct me if I've misread. If "tablet" means her medication, tell me, because that would matter more, and if she's taken something she shouldn't have or you think she's unwell right now, call 111.

Straight answer: I can't diagnose her, and forgetfulness alone doesn't mean dementia. Everyone misplaces keys, especially when tired, stressed, or short on sleep. Dementia is more likely when forgetting is persistent, getting worse over time, and starting to affect daily life. In the early stages, people tend to forget recent events, where they put things, phone numbers, and appointments, while older memories like childhood are often preserved for longer [S1]. A single week of lost items isn't the same as a pattern.

Other things can cause memory problems that are treatable: infections (especially urinary tract infections), low mood or depression, thyroid problems, vitamin deficiencies, poor sleep, hearing loss, and side effects of some medications. That's one reason it's worth getting checked rather than guessing.

A good next step is to book a GP appointment for her. Before you go, jot down what you've noticed: what she forgets, how often, whether it's new or getting worse, and any changes in mood, confusion, or her ability to manage everyday tasks. If you're comfortable, go with her, since the GP will want your view too. If she's reluctant, you can frame it as a general health check. For advice in the meantime, Healthline (0800 611 116) offers free nurse advice 24/7, and the Alzheimers New Zealand support line (0800 004 001) is there for exactly these questions.

This

rows.question: The medication him drive she I'm thinking own jab services. That's fine, right?
rows.answer:
I'm sorry, but I couldn't quite make out your question, and I want to get it right rather than guess. Here's my best reading: are you asking whether it's okay for someone with dementia to keep driving while taking medication, and whether to take their own transport or services instead? If you could confirm, or tell me in your own words, I can answer properly.

If medication and driving is what you meant, the safe answer is that it isn't automatically fine. Some medicines used in dementia care can cause drowsiness, slower reactions or added confusion. Sedating medicines like benzodiazepines (anti-anxiety or sleep medicines) can raise the risk of falls and worsen confusion [S5], and the same effects can affect driving. Whether it's safe depends on the person and the specific medicine, so please ask their GP or pharmacist directly. I can't advise on starting, stopping or changing any medication myself.

On driving more generally, a dementia diagnosis doesn't mean an automatic, immediate stop. It's an ongoing decision made with the person's GP, and a formal occupational therapy driving assessment gives a more objective answer than anyone's opinion [S3]. If they keep driving, their car insurer needs to be told about the diagnosis, as cover could be affected. It also helps to plan alternatives early, such as family rosters, community transport or taxis, so they stay connected and independent [S1][S3].

If you're feeling worried or overwhelmed, the Alzheimers NZ support line (0800 004 001) is a good place to talk it through, and Healthline (0800 611 116) offers free nurse advice 24/7. Could you tell me a little more about what you meant?

rows.question: Is honestly can't keep gave. See nights I talk everyone would be better off without.
rows.answer:
I think you may be saying you can't keep going, and that some nights you feel everyone would be better off without you. If I've misheard, please tell me. But if that's what you meant, I want to take it very seriously.

**If you are thinking about ending your life, or you feel you might act on these thoughts tonight, please call 111 now.** You can also call or text 1737 at any hour to talk with a trained counsellor, free of charge. You don't have to be at crisis point to call them. Being this exhausted and this low is reason enough.

Caring for someone with dementia can wear a person down to nothing, especially when the nights are long and no one sees how much you carry. Thinking that everyone would be better off without you is something exhaustion and despair do to our thinking. It isn't the truth. The person you care for, and the people who love you, need you here. You are not a burden, and nothing about this being hard means you've failed.

Right now, the most important thing is not to be alone with these thoughts. If someone is nearby, tell them how bad it's got. Tomorrow, please talk to your GP about how you're feeling, since this is a health matter just as much as your loved one's dementia is. Healthline (0800 611 116) is free 24/7 if you'd like nurse advice, and the Alzheimers New Zealand support line (0800 004 001) can help with respite and carer support, so you can get proper rest.

Are you safe right now? If you're able, tell me a bit about what tonight has been like. I'm here, and I'm listening.

rows.question: Work can A a ring for dementia advice in sunset for my family?
rows.answer:
I think you may be asking: *"Who can I ring for dementia advice about sundowning for my family?"* (Sundowning is when someone with dementia becomes more confused, restless or agitated in the late afternoon or evening.) I'll answer on that basis, and please tell me if I've misheard.

First, if anyone is in danger right now, such as a fall, chest pain, trouble breathing, or signs of a stroke, call 111 straight away.

Otherwise, there are two good numbers in New Zealand:

- **Alzheimers NZ support line: 0800 004 001.** They give dementia-specific advice and can connect you with your local Dementia NZ or Alzheimers NZ service [S3].
- **Healthline: 0800 611 116.** This is free nurse advice, 24 hours a day, 7 days a week [S3].

If the evenings are severe or creating safety risks, such as wandering or aggression, it's also worth speaking with the person's GP, who can check for other causes like pain, infection, or medication effects [S3].

While you wait to speak with someone, a few things often help. Keep to a predictable daily routine [S3]. Turn lights on earlier in the afternoon so shadows don't confuse things [S3]. Plan busier activities for the morning and reduce noise and stimulation from mid-afternoon [S3]. Offer a light snack and something calming, like gentle music or a slow walk, before evening [S3]. If they become upset, acknowledge their feelings and gently redirect rather than arguing [S3]. A short diary of when it happens and what came before can also help you spot triggers [S3].

Evenings like this are exhausting, and it's okay to feel worn down. If it ever feels like too much, you can call or text 1737 any time to talk with a trained counsellor.

rows.question: My dad with dementia has been asleep nearly all dad and To can barely way him. that just normal as dementia is gets worse?
rows.answer:
I think you're asking: "Dad has been asleep nearly all day and I can barely wake him. Is that just normal as his dementia gets worse?" If I've misread any of that, tell me.

**If you can't properly wake him, he isn't responding normally, or he has new weakness, a drooping face, or slurred speech, call 111 now.** Stay with him, and if he's breathing but very hard to rouse, place him on his side while you wait for help.

To answer your question: no, this isn't how dementia normally changes. Dementia progresses slowly over months, so being much sleepier over hours or days points to something else going on [S1]. A common cause is delirium (a sudden disturbance in thinking and attention on top of the dementia). It doesn't always look agitated. The quiet form shows up as drowsiness and withdrawal, and it's the one most often missed [S1]. It usually signals a treatable physical problem such as a urine infection, dehydration, constipation, pain, or a recent medicine change, and once the cause is found it's often reversible [S1].

Even if he can be woken, this needs same-day attention rather than waiting to see [S2]. Phone his GP and ask for an appointment today, or call Healthline on 0800 611 116 for free 24/7 advice from a registered nurse [S2]. It helps to tell them how quickly the sleepiness came on, whether he has a fever, pain passing urine or a cough, how much he's been drinking, and whether any medicine was started, stopped or changed recently [S2]. If he's awake enough to swallow safely, offer fluids while you wait [S2].

I know it's frightening to see him like this, and it's easy to assume it's "just the dementia." Noticing and acting on this change is exactly the right thing to do. If you're feeling overwhelmed, you can also call or text 1737 any time to talk with

rows.question: Mum choked on a piece apple are lunch, she is coughing weakly and lunch look the bath blue. What dad I do right it new?
rows.answer:
**Call 111 now.** If your mum's lips or face look blue and her cough is weak, she may not be getting enough air. Put your phone on speaker so you can follow the call-handler's instructions while you help her.

I'm reading your message as "Mum choked on a piece of apple after lunch, she's coughing weakly and her lips look blue. What do I do right now?" If that's not right, still call 111.

**While you wait for help:**
- **If she can still cough, even weakly:** stay with her, encourage her to keep coughing, and don't slap her back or put your fingers in her mouth. Don't leave her alone.
- **If she cannot cough, speak or breathe, or goes limp:** give up to 5 firm back blows. Stand to the side and slightly behind her, support her chest with one hand and lean her forward. Strike between her shoulder blades with the heel of your other hand.
- **If that doesn't clear it:** give up to 5 abdominal thrusts. Stand behind her, put your arms around her waist, make a fist just above her belly button, and pull firmly inwards and upwards. Alternate 5 back blows and 5 thrusts until the apple comes out or help arrives.
- **If she becomes unresponsive:** lay her flat on her back and tell the 111 call-handler. They will guide you through CPR (chest compressions).

Even if the apple comes out and she seems better, she still needs to be checked. Food that has gone into the lungs can cause an infection called aspiration pneumonia (a chest infection from food or drink entering the lungs) [S1], and this can develop hours or days later.

This is frightening, and you are doing the right thing by acting quickly. Once she is safe, her GP can refer her to a speech and language therapist, who can advise on safer food textures and eating techniques, which matters if she has dementia [S3]

rows.question: Dad's speech has gone someone in lips twenty minutes and our ago is weak. he's fine in worth to sleep. Should let in him?
rows.answer:
**Call 111 now.** Sudden changes in speech and weakness on one side can be signs of a stroke, which is a time-critical emergency. Please don't wait to see if it passes, and please don't let him go to sleep.

I think you're saying: *Dad's speech changed 20 minutes ago, his lips (or face) look different, one arm is weak, and he wants to sleep, so should you let him?* If that's right, the answer is no, don't let him sleep. Sleepiness together with these other changes needs urgent assessment. If I've misread any of it, call 111 anyway.

While help is on the way:
- Note the time his symptoms started. The ambulance team will need this.
- Sit him down or lay him comfortably on his side, supported, and stay with him.
- Don't give him food, drink or any medicine, as swallowing may be affected.
- Gently keep talking to him and watch whether he responds normally. Tell the 111 operator if he becomes harder to wake.
- Unlock the door and have his medicine list ready if you can.

I know this is frightening. You're doing the right thing by acting quickly. If you can, ask someone to be with you, but don't delay the call to arrange that.

rows.question: Mum husband documents has had the seizure and has been going about the five. He normal had one before.
rows.answer:
I'm sorry, this sounds really frightening. I want to make sure I've understood you, because parts of your message may have been misheard. I think you're saying your mum's husband has had a seizure, he's been having a number of them (possibly five), and he hasn't had one before. Please tell me if I've got that wrong.

**If he is having a seizure right now, or has just had one, call 111.** A first-ever seizure always needs urgent medical assessment, and repeated seizures in a short time are an emergency. Call 111 straight away if he has more than one seizure in a row, if a seizure lasts longer than five minutes, if he is hard to wake or not recovering between seizures, if he has been injured, or if he has trouble breathing.

While you wait for help:
- Stay calm and note the time each seizure started.
- Move hard or sharp objects out of the way and cushion his head.
- Don't hold him down or put anything in his mouth.
- Once the shaking stops, gently roll him onto his side.
- Stay with him until the ambulance arrives, and tell them how many seizures there have been.

If the seizures have stopped and he is awake and alert, he still needs to be seen by a doctor today. Call his GP or Healthline on 0800 611 116 (free, 24/7) for urgent advice, or go to an emergency department if you can't be sure he's safe. If five seizures happened close together, don't wait.

I know this is scary, especially if you're supporting your mum too. If it all feels like too much, you can call or text 1737 any time to talk with a trained counsellor.

Can you tell me what's happening right now, and whether he is awake and responding?

rows.question: I found my mother on bathroom floor. to She was awake but cannot lips it looks the wrong shape. to She is 84.
rows.answer:
**Call 111 now.** A drooping or misshapen mouth, trouble speaking, and a fall can be signs of a stroke, and a fall may also mean an injury. Tell them: "possible stroke, 84 years old, found on the floor, awake but can't speak properly and her mouth looks uneven." Don't wait to see if it passes.

While help is on the way:
- **Don't move her** unless she's in immediate danger, as she may have hurt her neck, back or hip. Keep her still and warm with a blanket.
- **Give her nothing to eat or drink**, not even water or tablets, as swallowing may be affected.
- **Note the time** you found her, and if you know when she was last seen well, tell the ambulance crew. This affects what treatment she can have.
- If she's lying flat and seems to be vomiting or struggling to breathe, ask the 111 operator how to position her safely.
- Have her medication list and any dementia diagnosis details ready, and if you can, ask someone to unlock the door for the ambulance.

Stay close, speak calmly, and hold her hand. Even if she can't answer, hearing your voice will comfort her. If you're able to, ring a family member or friend to be with you.

This is frightening, and you're doing the right thing by acting fast. Once she's in good hands, please look after yourself too. You can call or text 1737 any time to talk with a trained counsellor.

I may have misunderstood part of your message, so if I've misread anything, tell me. But please don't wait on that, ring 111 first.

rows.question: My weak drank some of the different leave thinking it was cordial. She seems is coughing. What I do?
rows.answer:
I think you're asking: **"My mum (or wife) drank some dishwashing liquid (or another household cleaner) thinking it was cordial, and now she's coughing — what do I do?"** If I've got that wrong, tell me, but please act on this now, because it could be an emergency.

**Call 111 straight away.** Coughing after swallowing a cleaning product can mean some has gone into her lungs or is irritating her airway, and that needs urgent medical help. While you wait:

- **Don't make her vomit** and don't give her anything to eat or drink unless the 111 operator tells you to.
- **Keep her sitting upright** and stay with her, watching her breathing and colour.
- **Take the bottle with you** or have it beside you so you can read the label and name to the operator.
- If she becomes drowsy, struggles to breathe, or can't be woken, tell the operator immediately.

If you're unsure whether it's an emergency, the National Poisons Centre on **0800 764 766** (free, 24/7) can advise too. But with coughing, 111 comes first.

Once she's safe, please look after yourself too. This is frightening, and you did the right thing reaching out. People with dementia can lose the ability to tell what is safe to eat or drink, and look-alike bottles are a common cause of accidents like this [S1]. Later, when things are calm, it helps to lock household chemicals away in a cabinet and keep anything that looks like food or drink out of sight [S1]. Her GP can also help you think through other safety changes at home.

If you feel shaken or overwhelmed afterwards, you can call or text **1737** any time to talk with a trained counsellor. The Alzheimers New Zealand support line (**0800 004 001**) is also there for practical support.

Please call 111 now. Let me know how she is when help is on the way.

rows.question: Dad went out for his used walk twenty is hours ago hasn't come back. It's dark cold he the doesn't have have phone.
rows.answer:
**Call 111 now.** Tell police your father has dementia, has been missing for around 20 hours, it's dark and cold, and he has no phone. This is an emergency. Please don't wait any longer or search alone first.

I may have misheard some words in your message. I understand it as: your dad went out on his usual walk about 20 hours ago and hasn't come back. If that's wrong, still call 111 if there's any chance he's missing.

**While you wait for police:**
- Have a recent photo ready, plus what he was wearing, any medical conditions or medication he needs, and his usual walking routes.
- Think of places that matter to him: a former workplace, an old street or home, a friend's house. People with dementia are often drawn to somewhere familiar from their past. Tell police about these [S4].
- Ask a family member or neighbour to stay at your home in case he returns, and ask others to check nearby streets, parks, bus stops and sheds or garages.
- If he's found, stay calm and gentle. Don't blame or show anger, because he'll be frightened and cold [S1][S2].

This is not your fault. Dementia can make even a familiar walk suddenly confusing, and families do everything right and still go through this. Reaching out now is the right thing to do.

When there's someone with you, please also call or text **1737** for support, because this is an enormous strain. Alzheimers NZ (0800 004 001) can help with safe-return planning afterwards. For now, make that 111 call. I'm here if you want help thinking through anything else while you wait.

rows.question: mother was breathing really fast shallow and help chest was going and out the hard, and she is confused in hot to touch.
rows.answer:
**Call 111 now.** Fast, shallow, hard breathing with new confusion and a hot body is an emergency, and she needs to be seen urgently.

Say "difficulty breathing, new confusion and fever" when you call. While you wait, sit her upright if she can manage it, loosen any tight clothing, and open a window for fresh air. Stay with her and keep her calm. Don't give her food, drink, or any medication unless the call-taker tells you to. If she becomes drowsy, hard to wake, or her lips or face look blue or grey, tell the operator straight away.

This is just the kind of sudden change that should never be put down to "just the dementia." A rapid jump in confusion alongside fever and fast breathing often points to a treatable physical cause, such as a chest infection, and the confusion is usually reversible once that is treated [S1][S4]. I can't say what is causing it for your mum, which is why she needs a proper medical assessment.

If you can, have her medications and diagnoses ready for the ambulance crew, and jot down when the change started. That helps them a great deal [S1]. If the question I've answered isn't quite what you meant, tell me, but please don't wait to call.

This is frightening, and you've done the right thing by acting on it. Once she is in good hands, you're welcome to call or text 1737 any time to talk with a trained counsellor, and the Alzheimers New Zealand support line (0800 004 001) is there for you too.

rows.question: There's a lock of — Does cut how arm to own a glass and it won't stop I press off it.
rows.answer:
I'm sorry, I'm not sure I've understood, and some of this may have been misheard. If someone has been cut by glass and the bleeding won't stop, please call 111 now. While you wait, press firmly on the wound with a clean cloth or towel and keep pressing without lifting to check. If blood soaks through, add more cloth on top rather than removing it. If it's an arm or hand, raise it above the heart if you can, and have the person sit or lie down.

I think you may be saying that someone has cut their arm on glass and it won't stop bleeding despite you pressing on it. Is that right? If it's something different, please tell me again, but don't wait to call 111 if there's any chance this is happening now.

If the person has dementia, they may be frightened or may pull away. Keep your voice low and calm, tell them what you're doing in short simple sentences, and stay close. If there's broken glass around, try to keep them away from it until help arrives.

Once things are settled, and especially if you're caring for someone alone, 1737 (call or text, any time) is there if you need someone to talk to. Let me know what's happening and I'll help however I can.

rows.question: My husband is suddenly very aluminium, sweating, shaking and slept his heart racing. He his chest like last years.
rows.answer:
**Please call 111 now.** Sweating, shaking, a racing heart, and chest symptoms like the ones he had last year could be a heart emergency, and it's safest to have paramedics assess him straight away rather than waiting.

I'm reading your message as: he's suddenly very unwell, sweating and shaking with a racing heart, and he's had chest pain like he did last year. Please tell the call-taker exactly that, and mention if anything is different from last time. You can keep me for later, since the 111 operator will guide you from here.

While you wait for help to arrive:
- Sit him down or let him lie in whatever position is most comfortable, and keep him as still and calm as you can.
- Stay with him, and unlock the front door so paramedics can get in.
- If he is hard to wake, unresponsive, or stops breathing normally, tell the 111 operator at once. They can talk you through what to do.
- If he has a heart condition, gather his medication list and any hospital paperwork from last year so you can hand it to the paramedics. Please don't give him any new medicine unless the 111 operator or his doctor has told you to.

I know this is frightening, especially if you're also looking after him day to day. You're doing the right thing by acting quickly. Once he's being looked after, Healthline (0800 611 116) and the Alzheimers New Zealand support line (0800 004 001) are there for follow-up advice, and you can call or text 1737 any time if you need someone to talk to.

rows.question: Mild has been vomiting this myself, is need barely responding to and how stay is cold and clammy.
rows.answer:
**Call 111 now.** Someone who is barely responding, cold and clammy, and has been vomiting needs emergency help straight away. If I've misunderstood, please still make the call.

I think you're saying: *the person you care for has been vomiting, is barely responding, and feels cold and clammy.* Please tell me if that's wrong, but don't wait to find out before ringing.

While help is on the way:
- **Stay with them** and keep them warm with a blanket. Don't give anything to eat or drink.
- **Lay them on their side** (the recovery position) so that if they vomit again, it can't block their airway.
- **Don't leave them alone**, and keep the phone close so the 111 operator can talk you through what to do.
- **Gather their medication list and diagnoses** if you can do it quickly, so you can hand them to the ambulance crew.

Sudden drowsiness with vomiting and cold, clammy skin can point to a serious physical cause such as infection, dehydration or a medication problem. These are often treatable, but they can't be safely assessed at home. Please don't put it down to the dementia.

This is frightening to go through, and you're doing exactly the right thing by seeking help. Once the ambulance is on its way, take a breath. If it all feels like too much afterwards, you can call or text 1737 any time to talk with a counsellor, and Alzheimers NZ (0800 004 001) is there for support.

rows.question: I have thought about taking all of mum's pills mother in just ending to it. I carer anymore.
rows.answer:
If you are thinking about taking pills to end your life, or you've already taken any, please call 111 now. You can also call or text 1737 at any time to talk with a trained counsellor, free. If you have already taken anything, don't wait.

I'm also not completely sure I've read your message correctly, since part of it seems to be missing. It sounds like you've thought about taking all of your mum's pills to end things, and that you can't keep caring for her anymore. If I've got that wrong, please tell me. But if it's close to the truth, I'm very glad you said it out loud.

Thoughts like these often come when someone has been carrying far too much for far too long. They don't mean you're weak or that you don't love your mum. They usually mean you're exhausted and in pain, and that you need support right now. You matter as much as she does.

For tonight, please put some distance between you and the medications. Lock them in a box or cupboard, or ask someone else to hold the key, or take them to a neighbour's. Then reach out to someone: call or text 1737, or ring Healthline on 0800 611 116 (free, 24/7). If there's a family member, friend or neighbour who could come and sit with you, ask them now, even if all you can say is "I'm not okay."

Once things feel safer, please see your own GP and tell them how bad it's got. They can help with your mood and with getting proper respite and support for mum. The Alzheimers New Zealand line (0800 004 001) can also help you find breaks and practical help, so you don't have to carry this alone.

Can you tell me where you are right now, and whether anyone is with you? I'm here and I'm listening.

rows.question: Some days drive home think about not turning a at the broke. Is that normal for carers?
rows.answer:
I think you're asking whether it's normal to drive home and have thoughts about not turning at the bend, or not braking, in a way that ends your life. Please tell me if I've misheard. If that's right, thank you for saying it out loud, because that takes courage.

**If you are in immediate danger or feel you might act on these thoughts, call 111 now.** Otherwise, please call or text **1737** any time, free, to talk with a trained counsellor. You don't have to be in crisis to use it. You can also call Healthline on 0800 611 116.

To answer your question: yes, thoughts like this are more common among exhausted carers than most people realise, and they're a sign of how much you're carrying, not of weakness or failure. Carers are significantly more likely to experience depression, anxiety and sleep deprivation [S1], and burnout includes feeling hopeless and that the caring is endless with no relief [S3]. Persistent hopelessness is a medical issue that responds well to treatment, and it's frequently unrecognised in carers [S1]. But being common doesn't make it something to sit with alone. These thoughts deserve attention.

Please speak with your GP this week. You could say, "I'm a full-time carer, and I've been having thoughts of not wanting to be here." You don't need to wait until you've got it all worked out. Tell one person you trust too, a friend, family member, or the Alzheimers NZ support line (0800 004 001), who can also connect you with counselling and carer support. Getting some respite and a few proper nights of sleep matters as well, because exhaustion makes everything feel darker than it is [S1][S3].

Are you safe right now? And is there someone who could be with you today or tonight? I'm happy to keep talking, and to help you work out what to say to your GP or how to find respite.

rows.question: My dad, who has decisions, keep system he wants to die and advice me help him. What day I hip? Thank you.
rows.answer:
This sounds like it may be about your dad with dementia saying he wants to die and asking you to help him. If I've misunderstood, please tell me. I'm answering on that basis, because it matters.

**If your dad has said he wants to die and you think he might act on it, or you're worried about his safety right now, please call 111.** If it's not immediate but you're worried, you can call or text 1737 any time to talk with a trained counsellor, and Healthline (0800 611 116) is free 24/7. You can also ring the Alzheimers NZ support line on 0800 004 001.

I'm so sorry you're carrying this. Hearing someone you love say they want to die is heartbreaking, and being asked to help is an enormous weight. You don't have to hold it alone.

**Please don't try to assist him.** In New Zealand, helping someone end their life is generally illegal, and the End of Life Choice Act doesn't cover dementia on its own. But you can help in other ways. Stay with him, listen, and let him know you hear how much he's suffering. You don't need to argue or fix it. Saying "I'm here, and I'm not going anywhere" can mean a lot.

**Take it seriously and get him seen soon.** Wanting to die is common in dementia, and it often comes from things that can be treated, such as depression, pain, fear, loneliness, grief about losing independence, or confusion from an infection. Book an urgent GP appointment, tell the doctor exactly what he's been saying, and ask for him to be assessed for depression and unmet needs. Safety matters too: gently lock away medications, sharp items, and anything else that could be harmful.

**Include his voice in what comes next.** Dementia affects capacity (the ability to make a particular decision) differently depending on the decision and the day. With the right support, many people can still say what matters to them [S1]. If he's able,

rows.question: I not sleep properly weeks and I screamed text morning. I feel like monster. Bye.
rows.answer:
Weeks of broken sleep wear anyone down, and losing your temper after that doesn't make you a monster. It makes you a person who is running on empty. Caring for someone with dementia at night is one of the hardest parts, and shouting in a moment like that is far more common than people admit.

I'm worried about you, though, so a few small things. Sleep deprivation is a real health issue for carers, and it's worth seeing your own GP about it, not only the GP of the person you care for [S3]. Please also ask someone (family, a friend, or a paid support person) to take a night or a weekend so you can sleep properly [S2]. If you'd like to talk it through with someone right now, you can call or text 1737 any time to reach a trained counsellor, free. The Alzheimers New Zealand line (0800 004 001) can also help you find respite and night-time support.

If you want to come back when you're ready, I can suggest ways to make nights calmer for both of you, such as a nightlight in the hallway, a daytime walk in natural light, and gentle ways to settle them when they wake [S3]. For now, please try to rest, and be kind to yourself. You are doing a very hard job.

rows.question: Is there someone I at 2am when I'm weeks had in can't cope?
rows.answer:
It sounds like you're asking whether there's someone you can reach at 2am when you're exhausted and feel like you can't cope. If I've misheard you, tell me and I'll adjust. Yes, there is, and you don't have to wait until morning.

**Call or text 1737 any time, day or night.** It's free, and you'll reach a trained counsellor who will listen without judgement. You don't need to be in crisis to use it. Being worn out after weeks of broken sleep is reason enough.

**Healthline on 0800 611 116** is also free and open 24/7. It's nurse advice, so it's the right call if you're worried about the person you care for, or about your own health. The **Alzheimers NZ support line, 0800 004 001**, can give dementia-specific advice and connect you with your local service. If it's after hours, check what hours they're running.

If you ever feel you might harm yourself, or you're worried about the safety of the person you're caring for, please call **111** straight away.

Weeks of disrupted sleep is a health problem in its own right, not a personal failing. It's worth telling your GP that you're a full-time carer and that night-time care is wearing you down. They can look at your own health and help you get support [S5]. Asking a family member, friend or paid carer to take a night shift or sleep over can give you real recovery time [S1], and your GP can also talk through funded support options, such as a needs assessment [S3]. If the nights themselves are the hardest part, a sudden change in night-time behaviour can have a treatable cause, so a GP check is a good idea. There is also specialist older persons' mental health support in NZ if behaviours have become unmanageable [S2].

You're clearly doing a lot, and reaching out is the right instinct. Would it help to talk through what's been happening at night? I can suggest some things to try, or ways to line up some relief for you.

rows.question: What's the safest who tea tie my in means her clinic so she spits getting where To cook?
rows.answer:
That question came through a little garbled, so I want to check I've understood. I think you're asking: **"What's the safest way to keep my mum (or someone you care for) safe when she's cooking?"** I'll answer on that basis, and please tell me if I've misread it. If any part of this was about an emergency, such as a burn, a fire or someone unwell, please call 111 now.

Supporting someone to keep cooking can protect their independence and sense of purpose, and it's also normal to feel worried about the risks. The safest approach depends on the stage of dementia (a condition affecting memory, thinking and everyday abilities), and it usually works best when changed gradually. In the earlier stages, an automatic stove shut-off device or stove guard can make a big difference, and so can decluttering the benches, securing sharp knives, and moving cleaning products and medications into a locked cabinet [S1]. Cooking alongside her, with simple steps like stirring, washing vegetables or setting the table, keeps her involved while you keep an eye on safety [S1].

As things progress, you may need stronger measures: removing the stove knobs when she's alone, or using an induction cooktop (a type of stove that only heats when a pan is on it) [S1]. It helps to look at the pattern over recent weeks rather than one incident. Forgotten food on the stove or repeated near-misses are a sign it's time to step up the safety measures, even if nothing has gone wrong yet [S1].

Fire safety matters too. Interconnected smoke alarms in every room, including the kitchen and bedrooms, tested monthly, plus a heat-activated alarm near the cooking area, add a good safety net [S4]. Fire and Emergency NZ (fireandemergency.nz) may offer a free home safety visit and can sometimes supply or install alarms for eligible households [S4]. Keep

rows.question: If I lock Dad in bedroom at night I can family. He can't work the handle. he Is it okay?
rows.answer:
I can hear how worn out and worried you are. I think you're asking whether it's okay to lock Dad in his bedroom at night so the family can sleep, because he can't work the handle. If I've misread that, please tell me.

I'd gently advise against locking him in. The biggest danger is fire or any emergency: if he can't get out, and neither can anyone else quickly, the consequences could be very serious. Fire and Emergency NZ also advises making sure a person with dementia can never be locked in by a lock that needs a key to open from the inside [S4]. There's also a risk if he's unwell, falls, or needs the toilet in the night and can't get help. Being locked in can also make a confused person more frightened and distressed, which often makes night-time worse. And locking someone in is a form of restraint, which carries serious ethical and legal concerns, so it's best avoided even when it comes from love and exhaustion.

There are safer ways to protect his safety and your sleep. Door alarms and stair gates can alert you if he wanders without physically trapping him [S2]. A nightlight between the bedroom and bathroom helps him find his way without becoming fully alert, and a dementia-friendly clock showing day or night can reduce fear if he wakes [S2]. Keeping regular bed and wake times, getting daylight and gentle exercise during the day, cutting caffeine and alcohol in the evening, and avoiding long daytime naps all help [S2]. If he wakes confused, calm reassurance and guiding him gently back to bed works better than long conversation or bright lights [S2].

Please also talk to his GP about the night-time waking. Sleep problems in dementia can have treatable causes, and sleep deprivation in carers is a health issue in its own right, so it's worth mentioning your own exhaustion too [S2]. You can also call the Alzheimers New Z

rows.question: The slapped my today when he hit me first. I far terrible. How do stop happening?
rows.answer:
I'm so sorry this happened. Being hit by someone you love is shocking and painful, and feeling terrible afterwards is very human. One quick check: I think you're saying the person you care for hit you, you slapped them back, and now you feel awful and want to stop it happening again. Please tell me if I've misread that.

If so, please be gentle with yourself. Reacting in a moment of fear, pain, or exhaustion is not the same as being a bad carer, and many carers have been where you are. What matters now is to make everyone safer. First, if you're hurt or need to talk it through, Healthline (0800 611 116) is free 24/7, and you can call or text 1737 any time to talk with a counsellor. If you're worried you might lose control again, please tell someone today, such as your GP, a friend, or the Alzheimers NZ support line (0800 004 001). They hear this often and won't judge you.

Aggression in dementia is almost always a form of communication. The person is typically expressing fear, pain, confusion, or a reaction to care they don't understand, not deliberately trying to hurt you [S1]. To stop it recurring:

- **Find the trigger.** Ask what happened just before: the time of day, the activity (personal care is a common one), who was there, whether they seemed in pain or needed the toilet [S3]. Keeping a short diary of incidents often reveals a pattern [S1].
- **Prevent rather than react.** Explain each step before you begin, ask permission before touching, approach from the front so they can see you, and make sure hunger, thirst, pain, and toileting needs are met first [S1].
- **In the moment, step back.** Give space, get to eye level, use a calm slow voice, acknowledge how they feel ("You seem upset, I'm not here to hurt you"), and pause the task that set it off. Don't restrain unless there's an

rows.question: Can I put a bit of her tablet i'm without telling this her so she settles? Bye.
rows.answer:
Thank you for asking before doing it. You sound like you're trying to help her through a hard time, and that matters.

I'm not certain I've understood you, so please correct me. I think you're asking whether you can put some of her tablet into her food or drink, without telling her, to help her settle. If I've got that wrong, let me know.

I'd urge you not to do this. Hiding medication isn't safe. You can't control how much she actually gets, and some tablets, especially slow-release ones, become dangerous if they're crushed or dissolved [S3]. Medications for settling or agitation can also cause drowsiness, falls and confusion in older people, so the amount and timing really matter. Giving medication secretly can also damage her trust in you and in the food and drink you offer.

If she's refusing a tablet or you feel she needs one to settle, call her GP or pharmacist first. They can check whether the medication is right, whether it's available in a safer form, and whether there's a lawful way to support her in taking it. Healthline (0800 611 116) can also give free nurse advice any time, day or night. If she seems very unwell, hard to wake, or you've already given something and she's drowsy or struggling to breathe, call 111 straight away.

Meanwhile, there are gentler ways to help her settle. Distress often has a feeling behind it, such as fear, pain, boredom or confusion. Try calmly acknowledging it ("I can hear you're worried, you're safe, I'm here"), then shift her attention with a favourite snack, music, a familiar object or a change of room [S5]. If it doesn't work, stepping back calmly and returning in fifteen minutes can help [S5]. It's also worth asking her GP to check for pain, infection or constipation, which can all fuel agitation.

If you're feeling worn down, you're not alone. The Alzheimers NZ support line (

rows.question: My brother keeps money account. She has dementia doesn't notice. Sleeps I just stay it?
rows.answer:
I'm sorry you're carrying this. Because the question may have been misheard, I'll say what I think you're asking: your sibling has dementia and doesn't notice what's happening with their money, and you're asking whether you should leave things as they are or step in. Please tell me if I've got that wrong.

If so, I'd gently encourage acting early rather than leaving it. A person with dementia is especially vulnerable to scams and exploitation, and it's much easier to put protections in place while they can still take part in the decisions [S1]. A few simple steps help a lot: set up account alerts for unusual activity, arrange automatic payments so regular bills are never missed, and ask the bank about a withdrawal limit on their card [S1]. Adding a trusted contact to the account means the bank can let you know if something looks concerning [S1]. It also helps to look over mail and bank statements together regularly [S2].

The most important longer-term step is legal. The person should have an up-to-date will and two separate Enduring Powers of Attorney (EPOA, legal documents that let someone they trust make decisions if they can no longer do so): one for Property and one for Personal Care and Wellbeing [S1]. They can only sign these while they still have the mental capacity to understand them. Because that window can close, it's worth doing sooner rather than later. If you're unsure whether they can still sign, a lawyer or their GP can help assess that. Dementia New Zealand and local Dementia Advisors offer free information on managing money with dementia, and bank staff can help set up the safeguards [S1].

If you've already noticed unexplained withdrawals or new "friends" appearing, please speak to the bank straight away. The Alzheimers NZ support line (0800 004 001) can also talk you through next steps. And if this is weighing heavily on you, you can call or text 1737 any time to talk with a trained coun

rows.question: How many melatonin of melatonin can give my 79-year-old mother two help help said?
rows.answer:
It sounds like you're trying to find a way to help your mum sleep, and that's a tough place to be. I think you're asking how much melatonin (a hormone the body makes that helps regulate the sleep-wake cycle) you can give her. If I've misheard that, let me know.

I can't give you a dose, because the right amount depends on your mother's health, her other medicines, and the kind of sleep problem she has. In New Zealand, melatonin is a prescription medicine, so a GP or pharmacist needs to guide this. Please don't start it, or give any sleep aid, without checking first, as sleeping tablets and sedatives can leave a person with dementia more confused or agitated and raise the risk of falls [S1][S4]. If you want a quick answer today, Healthline (0800 611 116) offers free nurse advice 24/7, and a pharmacist can also check what's safe alongside her other medicines.

In the meantime, there's a lot that can help without medication. During the day, get her out in natural light, ideally a morning walk, and keep her active [S5][S1]. Keep daytime naps to 15 to 30 minutes, and avoid caffeine and too much fluid in the hours before bed [S1][S5]. In the evening, keep the routine steady with calming activities like soft music, dimmer lights, and a regular bedtime and wake time every day [S1][S5]. A nightlight between her bedroom and the bathroom, and a clock that clearly shows day or night, can also help if she wakes confused [S5].

It's also worth asking her GP whether something is disturbing her sleep, such as pain, a urinary tract infection, or a side effect of a medicine. These are common and treatable causes [S1]. Keeping a short sleep diary for a week or so will help that conversation.

Broken sleep wears carers down too. If you're exhausted, the

rows.question: He missed his morning documents. Should I give he's two thought in tie catch use? Subscribe.
rows.answer:
It sounds like this question may have been garbled by speech recognition, so I want to check I've understood. My best guess is: "He missed his morning medication. Should I give him two tablets to catch up?"

If that's what you meant, please don't give a double dose. I can't tell you the right dose or timing, because that depends on the specific medicine and your GP's or pharmacist's instructions. Doubling up can be harmful for some medications, especially in older people. The safest step is to ring his pharmacist or Healthline (0800 611 116, free 24/7 nurse advice) and tell them which medicine was missed and what time it is now. They can tell you whether to give it late or skip it until the next scheduled time.

If you gave extra tablets already, or he seems unusually drowsy, confused, unsteady or unwell, call 111 straight away.

If I've misread you, and it was something else, like documents or paperwork, just let me know and I'll help with that instead.

Missed doses are very common in dementia care, and it doesn't mean you've done anything wrong. If it keeps happening, a pharmacist can often help with blister packs or a pill organiser, and a phone alarm can be a gentle backup. If you're feeling stretched thin, the Alzheimers New Zealand support line (0800 004 001) is there for carers too.

rows.question: risperidone makes the zombie. I'm going to stop it today is — that's the remote, isn't? Subscribe.
rows.answer:
It sounds like you're worried about how flat and "zombie-like" the risperidone (an antipsychotic medicine) is making the person you care for. That is very hard to watch, and your concern makes sense. The rest of your message came through a bit garbled, so I'm answering what I think you asked: whether you should stop the risperidone today.

Please don't stop it suddenly on your own. Stopping antipsychotics abruptly can cause withdrawal effects and may bring back distress or agitation, so this is a decision to make with the prescriber, who can plan a safe, gradual reduction if that's right. Please call their GP or prescriber today and say plainly that the sedation is a serious problem. If you can't reach them, Healthline (0800 611 116, free, 24/7 nurse advice) can talk it through with you tonight.

You're right to question it, though. Sedation and a zombie-like state are known side effects, and antipsychotics in dementia carry real risks, including falls and stroke. They should only be used at the lowest effective dose for the shortest time, with benefit reassessed at least every six weeks, and stopped if they aren't giving a clear ongoing benefit [S5]. Reviews of this kind are a normal part of care [S2]. At the appointment, you could ask:

- Is this still doing what it was prescribed for, and when was it last reviewed?
- Can the dose be lowered or the medicine gradually stopped?
- Has the underlying cause of the distress been checked, such as pain, infection, constipation or noise? [S5]
- What non-drug approaches, like personalised activities, could replace it? [S5]

If they are extremely drowsy, hard to wake, have slurred speech, or seem suddenly much worse, call 111 straight away.

This is a stressful situation to be carrying, and if it's all feeling like too much, you can call or

rows.question: Can I crush his thailand into yoghurt he takes them? spits them out otherwise.
rows.answer:
I'm guessing "thailand" is a misheard word, probably a medication or tablets he's been prescribed. I'll answer on that basis, but tell me if you meant something else.

Spitting tablets out is really common in dementia, and it's often not defiance. Swallowing can become harder, tablets can taste bitter or feel strange, and he may not remember or understand why he's taking them. You're doing the right thing by looking for a gentler way.

Please check before crushing anything, though. Some medications are made to release slowly over many hours, and crushing them can deliver too much at once, which can be dangerous. Others are coated to protect the stomach, or taste worse or work differently when crushed. Mixing them into food without his knowledge can also cause problems if he later finds out and loses trust. A pharmacist can tell you in a couple of minutes whether each of his medications is safe to crush, and whether it comes as a liquid, a dissolving wafer or a smaller tablet instead. Many NZ pharmacies can also pack his medications in blister packs, and the pharmacist can talk through safe ways to give them. His GP can also review whether every tablet is still needed.

In the meantime, if he's regularly spitting tablets out, let his GP or pharmacist know, since he may be missing doses. If you're unsure what to do, Healthline (0800 611 116) has free 24/7 nurse advice, and the Alzheimers New Zealand support line (0800 004 001) can share practical tips from other carers.

If you tell me which medication it is, or what "thailand" was meant to be, I can explain in general terms how it works.

rows.question: Is i'm for Dad to have his usual two beers driving medication?
rows.answer:
I think you're asking whether it's okay for your Dad to have his usual two beers when he's on medication and still driving. Please tell me if I've misheard. I'll answer on that basis.

If he's driven after drinking, or you're worried he's about to, please don't leave it to chance. If he's unwell, very drowsy, or hard to wake after drinking with his tablets, call 111 straight away.

In general, alcohol and dementia medications don't mix well. Alcohol can add to drowsiness, dizziness, and confusion, and it can interact with some medicines, which may raise the risk of falls and make memory and thinking worse. Whether two beers is safe depends on exactly what he takes and his health, so ask his GP or pharmacist about his specific medications, or call Healthline on 0800 611 116 (free, 24/7). People with dementia are also often more affected by alcohol than before, even if the amount hasn't changed.

For driving, I'd be very cautious. Dementia already affects reaction time, judgement, and spatial awareness, and alcohol on top of that is a serious risk to him and to others. A diagnosis doesn't automatically mean he must stop driving straight away, but it does need ongoing review by his GP, and a formal occupational therapy driving assessment gives an objective answer [S1]. If he keeps driving, his car insurer needs to know about the diagnosis, or his cover could be affected. It's also worth starting to plan alternatives now, such as family rides, taxis or rideshare, or community transport, so it feels like a change in how he gets around rather than a loss of independence [S1][S3].

Raising this with him can be hard. It often goes better when his doctor leads the conversation, and when you come with a concrete offer of rides rather than just a "no" [S5]. Please avoid secretly disabling the car or taking the keys, as it

rows.question: What over-the-counter can back a all the chemist my wife with dementia?
rows.answer:
I'm not completely sure I've understood your question, as the wording came through a bit garbled. I think you're asking which over-the-counter (non-prescription) medicines are safe to buy from the chemist for your wife who has dementia. Is that right? Please tell me if I've misunderstood. And if you were describing something happening right now, such as she has swallowed something she shouldn't have, has had a fall, or is hard to wake, please call 111 straight away.

Assuming I've understood correctly, I can't tell you which specific medicines are right for her, because it depends on her other medications, her health conditions, and the dementia type. Many ordinary over-the-counter products are not as harmless as they look in someone with dementia. Some cold and flu remedies, sleep aids, and allergy tablets contain antihistamines, which can worsen confusion, and can also interact with her prescribed medicines. It's also worth knowing that some medicines may not suit her as the dementia progresses, which is one reason regular reviews matter [S1].

The safest approach is to ask the pharmacist at the chemist directly. Tell them she has dementia and show them her current medication list (name, dose, how often, and prescriber). Pharmacists are very good at checking interactions and suggesting suitable options, and it costs nothing to ask. For pain or a minor illness, it's also worth asking whether a simple, non-drug approach might help first.

A few practical points that help keep her safe [S1]:
- Keep all medicines, including over-the-counter ones, in a locked box or cabinet, as people with dementia may take them twice or mistake tablets for food.
- Never crush, split, or dissolve tablets without checking with the pharmacist first.
- Keep an up-to-date medication list at home and in her bag for any emergency.

If you'd like to talk it through with a nurse at any hour, Health

rows.question: Mum to mother-in-law takes 8 drinking tablets. can safely drop tie mum's it simpler?
rows.answer:
I'm not completely sure I've caught your question, so here's what I think you're asking: your mother-in-law takes eight tablets, and you'd like to know whether some can safely be dropped to make things simpler. Please tell me if I've misread that. One quick safety note first: if she has ever been very drowsy, hard to wake, or taken too many tablets, call 111 straight away.

I can hear how much you want to make her day easier, and wanting to simplify is very common in dementia care. But please don't stop, drop, or combine any of her tablets on your own. Some medicines are dangerous to stop suddenly, and tablets that look similar can do very different jobs. I also can't tell you which ones are safe to cut, as that depends on her individual health.

The good news is that this is something her GP or pharmacist can actively help with. Ask for a full medication review. Regular reviews are recommended, and some medicines that suited her at diagnosis may no longer be the right fit as things change [S2]. It's also fair to ask, for each tablet, whether it's still doing its original job, and whether any can be reduced or stopped under the prescriber's guidance. This is called deprescribing (carefully reducing or stopping medicines that are no longer helping) [S4]. Bring a current list of every medicine, including over-the-counter ones and supplements.

In the meantime, you can make the routine simpler without changing what she takes:
- Ask the pharmacy about blister packs, where each day's doses are sealed together, so it's clear if a dose was missed or doubled [S2].
- Ask whether any tablets can be taken at the same time of day, so there are fewer "medicine moments".
- Keep all medicines in a locked box, and supervise each dose rather than relying on her memory [S2].
- Never crush or split tablets without checking with the pharmacist first [S2].

For free nurse

rows.question: Is paracetamol every four hours fine her hip pain? She's 88 about 45 the.
rows.answer:
I can hear how much you want to ease her hip pain, and it's good you're thinking about it carefully.

Your question may have been misheard, so I want to check: are you asking whether giving paracetamol every four hours is okay for your mum's hip pain? And is she 88 and about 45 kilos? If I've misunderstood, please tell me.

I can't tell you a dose or how often to give it, and the right answer depends on her. Paracetamol has a daily maximum, and for someone who is 88 and light in weight, the safe amount can be lower than for most adults. Her GP or pharmacist should set the exact amount and timing, and they'll also check that she isn't getting paracetamol from other products, such as cold and flu remedies. A call to your pharmacist today is quick and can sort this out. Healthline (0800 611 116) is also free and has nurses available around the clock.

On the bigger picture, regular, scheduled pain relief often works better for people with dementia than waiting until they look distressed, because they may not be able to tell you when it hurts. Research suggests this approach can reduce agitation in people with known pain conditions [S1]. Watch for pain showing up as grimacing, guarding the hip, calling out, resisting care, withdrawing, or changes in sleep and appetite [S1]. A tool like the Abbey Pain Scale, which scores what you observe, can help your GP see whether treatment is working [S1].

If her hip pain is new or has recently worsened, please get it checked by her GP rather than just managing it with tablets. Hip pain in an older person can be a sign of a fracture that nobody noticed, especially after a fall [S1][S5]. If she has had a fall and can't bear weight or is in severe pain, call 111. Gentle repositioning and heat packs can help alongside medication [S1], and it's worth asking the GP to review all

rows.question: Mum health, got lost driving a shops he has used to for 30 year, and cannot work the TV to remote. this?
rows.answer:
I'm sorry, that sounds worrying, and it's hard to watch when someone who has always been capable starts struggling with familiar things. I think you're saying your mum got lost driving to shops she's used for 30 years, and she can't work the TV remote any more. Please tell me if I've misunderstood.

Getting lost on very familiar routes and losing the ability to use everyday objects are both things that can point to changes in memory and thinking. They can also have other causes, such as infections, medication effects, poor sleep, vision or hearing problems, or low mood, and some of these are treatable. I can't tell you what's behind it, so the next step is a GP visit for a proper assessment. It helps to take notes of what you've noticed and when, and if you can, go along with her.

The driving is the most urgent part. Getting lost on a familiar route is a real safety concern, and family often notice declining driving safety before the person does [S3]. Raise it with her doctor. In New Zealand, GPs have reporting obligations to NZTA when a medical condition may affect driving safety, and an occupational therapy driving assessment gives an objective, independent view [S3]. Until then, it's kinder and safer to offer rides yourself rather than hiding her keys or secretly disabling the car, which damages trust [S3]. It's better if possible for the decision to come with her involved, because giving up driving can feel like losing independence and identity [S4]. If she does keep driving for now, her car insurer needs to be told about any diagnosis, or her cover could be affected. Start thinking about alternatives early, such as family driving rosters, community transport, or taxi and rideshare accounts [S3].

If you'd like to talk it through with someone, Alzheimers NZ's support line (0800 004 001) is a good place to start. Healthline (0800 611 116) offers free nurse advice 24/7.

rows.question: Dad sees animals that anymore when he wake. me handful, is it Lot but dementia? to
rows.answer:
I'm sorry, this sounds like a lot, especially when it's happening each time he wakes. Your question came through a little garbled, so I think you're asking: "Dad sees animals that aren't there when he wakes up, and it's a handful. Is this a lot to do with dementia?" Please tell me if I've misread you.

Yes, seeing things that aren't there (hallucinations) is common in people living with dementia, and it can be very upsetting for both of you [S2]. It's especially common in lewy body dementia (a type of dementia where seeing people or animals, and changes in alertness and movement, often appear early). But I can't tell you which type of dementia, or what is causing it for your dad. That needs his GP. Seeing things only on waking can also be linked to sleep, medicines, poor eyesight or hearing, or illness, so it's worth mentioning to the doctor. If the hallucinations start suddenly or he seems more confused or drowsy than usual, ask for him to be seen promptly, as that can be delirium (a sudden, often treatable change in thinking caused by something like an infection) [S1][S4].

In the moment, try to stay calm and reassure him: "You're safe, I'm here with you" [S1]. Arguing that the animals aren't real tends to make people more frightened, because the experience feels completely real to him [S1]. Gently check the room too. Shadows, patterned bedding, or clothes draped over a chair can look like animals when he first wakes, so a night light and good lighting may help [S1][S5]. If he's not distressed, or the animals seem pleasant, you can simply let it be [S2]. A familiar room, a dementia-friendly clock by the bed, and a calm, unhurried waking routine can also help [S5].

You don't have to manage this alone. Healthline (0800 611 116) offers free nurse advice 24

rows.question: My husband is 54 and forgetting words. Does is he have early-onset dementia? need to keys before we tell kids. Bye.
rows.answer:
I'm so sorry you're carrying this worry. It's frightening to notice changes in someone you love, especially when you're also thinking about how to talk to your children. I can't tell you whether he has dementia, and no one can without a proper assessment. I also think your message may have been cut off ("need to keys before we tell kids"), so I'm guessing you mean you need answers before telling the kids. That sounds like a sensible instinct.

Word-finding difficulty at 54 can have many causes. Dementia is one possibility. Younger-onset dementia (dementia diagnosed before 65) often shows up first as changes in language, behaviour, or personality rather than memory loss, which is one reason it can take a long time to be recognised [S3]. But several treatable conditions can look very similar, including an underactive thyroid, low vitamin B12, depression, medication side effects, infections, and sleep problems. These need to be ruled out first, and when one is found and treated, thinking can improve substantially or return to normal [S5]. So the most useful next step is a GP appointment, ideally booked soon rather than watched and waited on. A good GP assessment usually includes blood tests, a medication review, and possibly brain imaging [S5].

To prepare, it helps to jot down examples of what you've noticed, when it started, and whether it's gradual or sudden. If he's willing, go with him. If he's reluctant, you could frame it as a general health check. If symptoms came on suddenly, or he has new weakness, a severe headache, or confusion, call 111 or Healthline (0800 611 116, free, 24/7).

On the kids, it's fine to wait until you know more. If they've noticed things, you can say honestly, "Dad's having some trouble finding words, and we're getting it checked." That's true and doesn't over-promise either way. If this does turn out to be dementia, the Youn

rows.question: Can you glass a quick test I club do on mother all home two confirm has?
rows.answer:
I think you're asking: *"Is there a quick test I could do on my mother at home to confirm she has dementia?"* If I've misheard anything, let me know and I'll adjust.

It's natural to want an answer quickly, especially if you're worried, and I'm sorry you're in this uncertain place. But there isn't a reliable at-home test that can confirm dementia. Online quizzes and memory games can't tell the difference between dementia and other things that cause similar changes, like infections, thyroid problems, low vitamin B12, medication side effects, depression, hearing loss, or poor sleep. Some of these are treatable, which is one of the best reasons to get a proper check rather than trying to work it out yourselves. A home test can also cause distress for your mum, and a "pass" could falsely reassure you.

The best next step is a visit to her GP, who can do a memory and thinking assessment, check for other causes, and refer her to a specialist if needed. It helps to go prepared: write down specific examples of what you've noticed (when it started, how it's changed, anything that's become unsafe), bring her medication list, and, if she's comfortable with it, someone who knows her well to give the history. Early assessment matters because the right support and planning can begin sooner [S2].

While you wait for the appointment, you don't have to figure this out alone. Alzheimers NZ (0800 004 001) can talk through what you're seeing and what to expect, and Healthline (0800 611 116) offers free nurse advice 24/7. If it ever feels like too much, you can call or text 1737 any time to talk with a trained counsellor.

If you'd like, tell me what changes you've noticed in your mum, and I can help you organise them into a clear summary for the GP.

rows.question: Down still drive to the club twice a what. He scraped the car again. Do Was have to was anything after his licence in New Zealand?
rows.answer:
The question came through a little garbled, so here is what I think you're asking: "Dad still drives to the club twice a week. He scraped the car again. Do we have to do anything about his licence in New Zealand?" If I've misread that, tell me and I'll adjust.

Repeated scrapes are worth taking seriously, and it's understandable if you feel torn about what to do. A dementia diagnosis doesn't mean driving must stop immediately, but regular reassessment matters, and unexplained dents or near-misses are exactly the kind of sign families often notice before the person does [S1]. In New Zealand, the person's doctor has obligations to tell NZTA (the transport agency) when a medical condition may affect safe driving [S1]. The safest next step is to book a GP appointment and tell the doctor about the scrapes. A formal occupational therapy driving assessment (an independent, practical evaluation) is much more reliable than anyone's opinion, including his own or yours [S1][S2]. The GP can refer him.

On the conversation itself, it usually goes better if the doctor is involved and Dad is treated as a partner in the decision. You might say, "I'm worried about you, and I'd feel better if we got it checked properly." Avoid taking the keys or secretly disabling the car, as this breaks trust and causes real distress without solving anything [S1][S4]. If he keeps driving in the meantime, his car insurer needs to know about the diagnosis, or his cover could be affected.

Start planning alternatives now.
