rows.question: dad dementia back asleep nearly all I become wake him. Is it just normal are dementia worse?
rows.answer:
I'm sorry, this sounds worrying. I think you're asking: your dad, who has dementia, is now asleep nearly all the time and hard to wake, and you want to know whether this is normal or the dementia getting worse. Please tell me if I've misread that.

**If you can't wake him properly, he's not responding normally, he's collapsed, or he has new weakness, a drooping face, or slurred speech, call 111 now.** Don't wait to see if it passes.

If he can be woken but is far sleepier than usual, this is not how dementia normally changes. Dementia progresses over months, so sleepiness that has come on over hours or days is usually a sign of something else. A common cause is delirium (a sudden change in thinking and alertness, layered on top of the dementia). The quiet form of delirium shows up as drowsiness and withdrawal rather than restlessness, and it's the form most often missed [S2]. It usually points to a treatable physical problem such as a urinary infection, dehydration, constipation, pain, or a recent medicine change [S2]. It can look as though the dementia has jumped forward overnight, but once the cause is found and treated, delirium is usually reversible [S2].

Please get same-day medical advice. Call his GP and ask for an appointment today, or ring Healthline on 0800 611 116 (free, 24/7, registered nurses) [S3]. It helps to tell them how quickly the sleepiness came on, any fever, pain passing urine or cough, how much he's been drinking, and whether any medicine was started, stopped or changed recently [S3]. While you wait, keep him safe and comfortable, and offer fluids only if he's awake enough to swallow safely [S3].

You're not overreacting by checking, and you're not to blame for not knowing. This is a hard thing to watch. If it's all getting too much, you can call

rows.question: Mum choked on a piece apple are lunch, she is coughing weakly and lunch look the bath blue. What dad I do right it new?
rows.answer:
**Call 111 now.** I'm reading this as: Mum choked on a piece of apple, she's coughing weakly, and her lips look blue. If that's right, this is an emergency. Put the phone on speaker so the call-taker can talk you through it while you act.

**While you wait for help:**

- **If she can still cough, even weakly:** encourage her to keep coughing. Don't slap her back yet, and don't put your fingers in her mouth.
- **If she can't cough, speak or breathe, or goes limp or silent:** lean her forward, support her chest, and give up to 5 firm blows between her shoulder blades with the heel of your hand. If that doesn't clear it, give up to 5 abdominal thrusts: stand behind her, fist just above her belly button, pull sharply inwards and upwards. Alternate back blows and thrusts until it comes out or help arrives. The 111 call-taker can guide you.
- **If she becomes unresponsive and stops breathing,** lower her to the floor and start CPR (pressing hard and fast in the centre of her chest). The call-taker will coach you.

Even if the apple comes out and she seems to recover, she still needs to be checked. Food or fluid can slip into the lungs, and that can lead to a serious chest infection (aspiration pneumonia) hours or days later. Choking in someone with dementia can also be a sign that swallowing is getting harder, which is worth raising with her GP afterwards.

You're doing the right thing by acting fast. Please call 111 now. Once Mum is safe, I'm here to help with what comes next, including safer food textures and swallowing assessment.

rows.question: Dad's speech has gone someone in lips twenty minutes and our ago is weak. he's fine in worth to sleep. Should let in him?
rows.answer:
**Call 111 now.** Sudden changes in speech and weakness can be signs of a stroke, and every minute counts. Please don't let him go to sleep and wait to see how he is.

I'm reading your message as: *"Dad's speech has gone, something in his lips for twenty minutes, and our arm is weak (his arm is weak). He's fine but wants to sleep. Should I let him?"* If I've misunderstood, please still call 111, as it's safer to be checked and told it's nothing.

While you wait for the ambulance:

- **Stay with him** and keep him calm and comfortable, sitting or lying down with his head supported.
- **Don't give him food, drink or any tablets**, as swallowing may not be safe right now.
- **Note the time** the symptoms started (about twenty minutes ago), because the ambulance crew and hospital will need it.
- **Try to keep him awake and talking if you can.** If he becomes hard to wake, tell the 111 operator straight away.
- **Unlock the door** and have someone ready to meet the ambulance, plus a list of his medicines if you can grab it.

The call-taker will guide you through everything, so just answer their questions as best you can. You're doing the right thing by acting quickly, and I know this is frightening. Once he's in safe hands, you can call or text **1737** any time to talk with a trained counsellor if you need support.

rows.question: Mum husband documents has had the seizure and has been going about the five. He normal had one before.
rows.answer:
I'm sorry, this sounds frightening. Some of your message may have been misheard, so I want to check I've understood.

**If he is having a seizure right now, is unresponsive, is hard to wake, or has hurt himself in a fall, please call 111 straight away.** Stay with him, keep him safe, and don't put anything in his mouth.

I think you may be saying: *"My mum's husband has had a seizure, and it's been going on for about five (minutes?), and he's never had one before."* Please correct me if I've got that wrong, especially about the five. Was it five minutes, five seizures, or something else?

If it was a first-ever seizure lasting around five minutes, or it's still going, or one seizure is following another, that is an emergency, so please call 111 now. If it has stopped but he's still confused, drowsy, or not back to himself, please call 111 as well. A first seizure always needs urgent medical assessment, even if he seems to recover. In older adults, a new seizure can be linked to things like a stroke, infection, a fall or head knock, or changes in the brain, and only a medical team can work out the cause. If he's had a seizure and has dementia, tell the paramedics or doctors, as they'll want to know about his medications and any recent changes.

While you wait for help, gently turn him onto his side once the shaking stops, loosen anything tight around his neck, note the time the seizure started and how long it lasted, and stay calm and close to him. Please also look after yourself. If you or your mum are feeling overwhelmed, you can call or text 1737 any time to talk with a trained counsellor.

Let me know what you meant by "the five" and where things are at right now, and I'll help from there.

rows.question: I mother on the bathroom feel. cannot mum's your and the words stay. She 84.
rows.answer:
If your mum has fallen in the bathroom and may be hurt, please call 111 now. Don't try to lift her or move her. Stay with her, keep her warm with a blanket or towel, and speak calmly. If she's unresponsive, hard to wake, struggling to breathe, or has sudden facial droop, slurred speech or arm weakness, tell the call-taker straight away.

I may have misheard your message, so I'll say what I think you meant: your 84-year-old mum has fallen on the bathroom floor, and you can't get her up. Is that right? If it's something different, let me know.

While you wait for help, sit or kneel beside her at her level and use a soft, unhurried voice. Even if she doesn't take in your words, she'll pick up on your tone and your calm presence. Gentle touch on her hand can reassure her, as long as she seems comfortable with it [S5]. If she doesn't recognise you or seems confused, simply say something like "Hello Mum, I'm here, help is coming" rather than correcting her [S3]. Please don't try to stand her up yourself, even if she says she's fine, because people with dementia may not feel or report an injury straight away [S4].

After any fall, she should have a medical review, and an occupational therapy home assessment (a visit from a specialist who recommends safety changes at home) can help prevent another one. Grab rails, non-slip mats, good lighting and a nightlight are common changes [S4]. For advice afterwards, Healthline (0800 611 116) is free 24/7, and the Alzheimers NZ support line (0800 004 001) can help too. This is a frightening moment, so if you need someone to talk to, you can call or text 1737 any time.

Is she conscious and talking to you? Tell me what you're seeing and I'll stay with you.

rows.question: My weak drank some of the different leave thinking it was cordial. She seems is coughing. What I do?
rows.answer:
**Call 111 now.** If this is what I think it is, swallowing a household cleaning product is a medical emergency, and coughing can mean some has gone into her lungs.

I think you said: "My wife drank some of the dishwashing liquid thinking it was cordial, and now she is coughing." Please tell me if I've misheard, but treat it as an emergency until you know otherwise.

While help is on the way:
- **Do not make her vomit.** This can burn her throat again and send the liquid into her lungs.
- **Don't give food or drink** unless the 111 operator tells you to, as they may advise a small sip of water in some cases.
- Sit her upright and stay with her, watching her breathing.
- Keep the bottle, so the ambulance crew and doctors know exactly what she swallowed.
- You can also call the **National Poisons Centre on 0800 764 766** (free, 24/7), but call 111 first if she is coughing, struggling to breathe, or drowsy.

Coughing after swallowing a liquid can mean it has gone down the wrong way, into the lungs instead of the stomach, which can cause a serious chest infection called aspiration pneumonia [S1]. That is why she needs to be checked even if she seems to settle.

Once she is safe, please take care of yourself too. This is frightening, and it is not your fault. People with dementia can lose the ability to tell what is edible and what isn't, so a bottle that looks like a drink can be mistaken for one [S1]. Afterwards, it will help to lock household chemicals in a cupboard and keep them out of sight [S1]. If you feel shaken or overwhelmed, you can call or text 1737 any time to talk with a trained counsellor, and the Alzheimers New Zealand support line (0800 004 001) is there once things have calmed down.

rows.question: Dad went his usual ago and hasn't come. drop and cold in he doesn't have phone.
rows.answer:
**Please call 111 now** if your dad hasn't come home, it's cold, and he has no phone. With dementia, being missing in the cold is an emergency, so don't wait to see if he turns up. (I think you're saying he went out on his usual walk, hasn't returned, and it's cold. If I've misread anything, still call 111 first.)

When you call, ask for police and tell them he has dementia. Have ready:
- A recent photo and what he's wearing
- Which way he normally goes, and where he might head (an old workplace, a former home, somewhere meaningful to him)
- Any medical conditions or medication he needs

While you wait, ask a neighbour or family member to check his usual route and nearby places he knows, and keep one person at home in case he returns. Check around the house, garage and garden too. Keep your phone free so police can reach you. Don't drive off alone if it means leaving no one at the house or being unreachable.

When he's found, stay calm and gentle. He may be frightened or confused, so reassure him and avoid blame or anger [S2]. If he seems very cold, drowsy or unwell, tell the paramedics or police right away.

This is frightening, and you're doing the right thing by acting quickly. Once he's safe, it's worth planning ahead: an up-to-date photo, ID he can carry, a note of his usual routes and meaningful places, and working out the times he's most likely to walk [S2]. Alzheimers New Zealand (0800 004 001) can help you put practical safeguards in place, and you can call or text 1737 any time if you need to talk to someone tonight.

Please call 111 now, and let me know when he's home.

rows.question: My mother is really chest i gone in and out, and confused and touch.
rows.answer:
I'm sorry, this sounds frightening. I think you may be telling me your mother has a chest problem, is drifting in and out of consciousness, is confused, and is hard to wake or respond to. Please correct me if I've misheard.

**If that's right, call 111 now.** Chest pain or breathing difficulty, being "in and out," and new confusion can signal a medical emergency, such as a serious infection, stroke, heart problem or breathing trouble. Don't wait to see if it passes. While help is on the way:

- Stay with her and keep her as comfortable as you can, ideally sitting up a little or lying on her side if she's drowsy.
- Don't give her food, drink or any tablets unless the 111 call-taker tells you to.
- If she becomes unresponsive or stops breathing normally, tell the call-taker straight away. They can guide you step by step.
- Have her medication list and any diagnoses ready for the ambulance crew, and note when the change started.

A sudden change over hours or days, with much more confusion than usual, is never "just the dementia getting worse." It almost always points to a treatable physical cause, such as a chest infection, urinary infection, dehydration or pain [S4]. Getting her seen quickly gives her the best chance of recovery.

You're doing the right thing by paying attention. If it turns out she's more settled than I'm picturing, Healthline (0800 611 116) offers free 24/7 nurse advice, but if she's hard to wake or struggling to breathe, 111 is the right call. Afterwards, if you feel shaken or overwhelmed, you can call or text 1737 any time to talk to a trained counsellor.

Could you tell me if I've understood this correctly, and how she's doing right now?

rows.question: There's a lot blood — Dad cut arm our a glass won't stop bleeding even I press it.
rows.answer:
**Call 111 now.** Heavy bleeding that won't stop with pressure is an emergency. Put the phone on speaker so you can keep your hands on the wound while you talk to them.

While you wait for help:
- **Keep pressing hard and steadily** directly on the cut with a clean cloth, towel or tea towel. Don't lift it to check. If blood soaks through, put more cloth on top and keep pressing.
- **Raise the arm** above the level of his heart if you can.
- **Get him sitting or lying down.** Blood loss can make him faint, and lying flat with his legs raised a little helps.
- **If there's glass still in the wound, don't pull it out.** Press around it, not on it.
- If he's on blood thinners, mention that to the 111 operator.

Dad may be frightened or confused, especially if he has dementia. Speak calmly, stay close, and tell him simply what you're doing: "I'm helping you, Dad. Help is coming." If he tries to pull away, keep your voice gentle and keep the pressure on as best you can.

You're doing the right thing by acting fast. Stay on the line with 111 and follow their instructions. Once he's safe, I'm here if you want to talk through what happened or how to make things safer at home.

rows.question: My husband suddenly very in agitated, sweating, school says heart racing. had chest pain like last year.
rows.answer:
**Call 111 now.** Sudden agitation, sweating, a racing heart and chest pain (especially with a past episode of chest pain) could be a heart emergency, and it needs an ambulance rather than waiting to see how it goes. I'm reading "school says" as "he says" his heart is racing. If that's wrong, please still call, as the symptoms you describe are enough.

While you wait for help:
- Have him sit or lie down in whatever position is most comfortable, and keep him as calm and still as you can. Speak slowly and quietly, and stay close.
- Unlock the front door and, if you can, ask someone to wait outside for the ambulance.
- Gather his medication list and any chest-pain or heart medicines he's prescribed, and tell the call-taker about his dementia. The call-taker may suggest other steps for you to take, so follow their guidance.
- Don't give him food or drink or anything new, and don't let him walk around or go to the toilet alone.
- If he becomes unresponsive or stops breathing normally, tell the 111 call-taker straight away, as they can talk you through what to do.

I know this is frightening, and with dementia it can be hard to tell what's pain, what's fear and what's confusion. You don't need to work that out. Sudden agitation in someone with dementia can come from a physical cause, and chest pain with sweating needs checking by paramedics either way.

Once he is safe and in the hands of the ambulance crew, it's worth having someone stay with you, because this is a lot to carry alone. If you're feeling overwhelmed afterwards, you can call or text 1737 any time to talk with a trained counsellor, and Alzheimers New Zealand (0800 004 001) is there for support too.

Please call 111 now. I'm here if you want to tell me how it's going.

rows.question: Mum hard been vomiting this morning, now responding to mum and skin is cold.
rows.answer:
**Call 111 now.** Vomiting followed by not responding and cold skin could be a medical emergency, so please don't wait. (I think you meant "now *not* responding to Mum", so tell me if I've misread.)

While you wait for the ambulance:
- Stay with her and keep her warm with a blanket, without overheating her.
- If she's lying down, gently roll her onto her side, with her top knee bent, so any further vomit can drain from her mouth and doesn't block her breathing.
- Don't give her anything to eat or drink.
- Check whether she's breathing. If she stops breathing normally, the 111 call-taker will guide you through what to do, so keep the phone on speaker beside you.
- Have her medication list and diagnoses ready for the paramedics, and note roughly when the vomiting started and when she stopped responding.

A sudden change like this is never "just the dementia," and it often has a treatable physical cause that needs prompt medical care [S1]. The 111 team will tell you exactly what to do next.

This is frightening, and you're doing the right thing by acting quickly. Once she's in safe hands, please consider calling or texting 1737 any time to talk with a trained counsellor, and lean on whānau or friends to be with you.

rows.question: have after taking all mum's and effects it. I can't do i this.
rows.answer:
I'm so sorry. It sounds like you're in a really hard place right now, and I want to make sure I understand you properly. The message came through a bit jumbled, so I'm not certain what you meant.

If you or your mum have taken something that could be harmful, or if you're having any thoughts of hurting yourself, please call 111 straight away. Stay on the line, and if your mum has taken medication that wasn't meant for her (or too much of her own), tell them exactly what and roughly how much. Healthline (0800 611 116) can also advise on medication concerns 24/7, but 111 comes first if anyone is unwell or unsafe.

My best guess is you may be saying you're exhausted and feel you can't keep going with caring for your mum, or that something has happened with her medication and its effects. Could you tell me which it is? I'll answer whichever you meant.

And if it's the second kind of "I can't do this", the kind where caring has become too much, please know that feeling is real and very common, and it doesn't make you a bad daughter or son. You can call or text 1737 at any time to talk with a trained counsellor, and the Alzheimers NZ support line (0800 004 001) can help you find respite and support so you're not carrying this alone.

I'm here. Tell me what's happening and we'll work through it together.

rows.question: Was drive home think aren't not turning. Is that normal for carers?
rows.answer:
I'm not sure I've caught your question properly, so let me check. I think you may be asking: "On the drive home, I was thinking I don't want to turn (into our street / go home). Is that normal for carers?" If I've misheard, tell me and I'll answer again.

If you are driving right now and feeling unsafe to be on the road, please pull over somewhere safe. And if any part of this involves thoughts of harming yourself, please call 111 straight away. You can also call or text 1737 at any time to talk with a trained counsellor, and they are there for exactly this.

Whatever the exact words were, what you're describing is very common. Many carers dread going home, or catch themselves wishing they could keep driving, just for a little quiet. It doesn't mean you don't love the person you're caring for or that you're a bad carer. It's usually a sign of exhaustion, because burnout (a state of physical, emotional and mental exhaustion from sustained caregiving) is a predictable result of high-intensity care without enough relief, not a personal failing [S4]. Warning signs include fatigue that doesn't ease with rest, feeling hopeless or resentful, and withdrawing from things you used to enjoy [S4].

Please don't carry this alone. Take up offers of respite care, consider a carer support group through Carers NZ (carers.net.nz) or your local Alzheimers NZ service, and tell your GP you're a full-time carer, since depression and anxiety in carers are common and respond well to treatment [S4][S5]. You can also call the Alzheimers NZ support line on 0800 004 001, or Healthline on 0800 611 116 for free nurse advice any time.

If you'd like, tell me a bit more about what's been happening and I'll help you think through some practical next steps.

rows.question: My dad, shallow hob wants and mum the he's him. do to hard?
rows.answer:
I'm sorry, but I couldn't quite make out your question. It looks like some words may have been lost or misheard, and I don't want to guess wrongly.

If anything you're describing is happening right now and could be an emergency, such as a fall, trouble breathing, signs of a stroke, or someone being hard to wake, please call 111 straight away.

Here's my best guess at what you might be asking: **"My dad has dementia and he doesn't recognise Mum (or me), or he's being difficult with her. What can we do? It's so hard."** Is that close? If so, here's a little to hold onto in the meantime.

If your dad no longer recognises your mum, that is a symptom of the disease, not a reflection of their relationship or what it has meant. Many people with dementia still respond warmly to people they can't name. A calm, simple introduction ("Hello love, it's Anne, I've come to sit with you") tends to work better than correcting him ("It's me, your wife!") [S3]. And if he's resisting help with personal care or pushing someone away, it often helps to have a familiar person present and give him plenty of time to get comfortable [S1].

Whatever the exact situation is, it sounds like things are hard, and that is completely understandable. Could you tell me again in a few words what's been happening? In the meantime, the Alzheimers NZ support line (0800 004 001) is a good place to talk it through with someone who understands. If you're feeling overwhelmed yourself, you can call or text 1737 any time to talk with a trained counsellor.

rows.question: I not in I shuffles mother morning. I feel your last the.
rows.answer:
I'm sorry, but I'm having trouble making out your message. It may have been misheard by the speech recognition, or something may have been cut off along the way. I'd rather check than guess.

Could you tell me again, in a few simple words, what's happening with your mother? For example, is she having trouble in the mornings, such as shuffling when she walks, not recognising you, or something else? Or is there a feeling you'd like to talk through?

If your mother has fallen, is hard to wake, has sudden weakness or slurred speech, or is having trouble breathing, please call 111 straight away.

And if you're feeling overwhelmed or very low yourself, you can call or text 1737 at any time to talk with a trained counsellor. You can also reach the Alzheimers New Zealand support line on 0800 004 001 for a friendly, understanding ear. I'm here whenever you're ready to try again.

rows.question: saying can text 2am when I'm sitting out with help I can't cope?
rows.answer:
I'm sorry it's so hard right now. Sitting up at 2am, exhausted and feeling you can't cope, is one of the loneliest places a carer can be. Reaching out is the right thing to do.

I may have misheard part of your message, so let me check: are you asking whether you can text someone for support in the middle of the night when you're feeling you can't cope? If so, yes. You can call or text 1737 any time, day or night, and talk with a trained counsellor. It's free, and you don't need to be in crisis or have the "right" words. Saying "I'm caring for someone with dementia and I'm at the end of my rope" is enough.

If you're having thoughts of harming yourself, or you're worried about your safety or the safety of the person you care for, please call 111 now.

If the person you care for is awake and unsettled, a few things can help while you get through tonight. Stay calm, keep the lights low, and check whether they need the toilet, a drink, or a snack. Calming music, a blanket, or sitting quietly with them can help too [S2]. Try not to argue or correct them. Acknowledge how they feel and gently guide them back toward rest [S3].

For tomorrow, when you've had a little rest, Alzheimers NZ's support line (0800 004 001) can talk through your situation and connect you with local help, including respite so you can sleep. Healthline (0800 611 116) gives free nurse advice 24/7 if you're worried about them or yourself tonight. It's also worth seeing their GP, since broken sleep can have a treatable cause like an infection, pain, or a medication effect [S2], and a GP can refer to older persons' mental health services if the nights are becoming unmanageable [S5]. Accepting help isn't failing. Carers who accept it tend to stay well and care better for longer [S4].

Are you okay right now? If you tell me

rows.question: safest way to my mother into your chair stops while cut?
rows.answer:
If your mother has fallen, is hurt, is bleeding heavily, or can't be woken, call 111 now. I'm not certain I've understood your question, as it may have been misheard. I think you're asking: **"What's the safest way to help my mother into a chair, and how do I stop her from falling while I do it?"** If that's not right, please tell me and I'll adjust.

Assuming it is, you're right to think about this carefully, because transfers are a common cause of injury for both the person and the carer. The safest approach is to use your mother's own remaining strength rather than lifting her weight. If she can stand and follow simple instructions, guide and support her rather than lift [S1]. Give one clear instruction at a time ("Shuffle forward... hands on the arms... now stand"), and give her time to respond before moving on [S1]. Stand close, keep your feet apart, your back straight, and bend at your knees [S1]. Make sure the chair is stable, ideally with arms, and positioned close so she only has to turn a little.

If she begins to fall, don't try to catch her. Guide her down gently and call for help, as trying to catch someone is a leading cause of carer injury [S1]. If she does fall, don't try to lift her yourself. Check whether she's hurt, and call 111 if you suspect an injury, she hits her head, or she can't get up safely. Even after a minor fall, arrange a medical review with her GP [S2].

If she can't safely bear her weight, please don't keep trying manual lifts. An occupational therapist (a health professional who assesses everyday movement and equipment needs) can recommend slide sheets, transfer boards, or hoists, and a community physiotherapist can teach you safe handling technique [S1]. Her GP, or Alzheimers NZ (0800 004 001), can help arrange an assessment. Healthline (0800

rows.question: I'm I Dad his bedroom night Out sleep. He is can't work the handle. okay?
rows.answer:
That sounds like a really worrying and exhausting situation, and I want to make sure I've understood you. I think you're asking: **"My dad has dementia and I'm thinking of locking him in his bedroom at night so he can't wander. He can't work the door handle. Is that okay?"** If I've got that wrong, let me know and I'll answer again.

If that's the question, I'd gently advise against locking him in. If there were a fire, a fall, a medical problem, or he needed the toilet and became frightened or distressed, he couldn't get out and you might not reach him in time. Being trapped can also increase panic, confusion and agitation, which often makes night-time restlessness worse. In New Zealand, locking someone in is also considered a form of restraint, which carries real safety, ethical and legal concerns.

There are safer ways to keep him from wandering at night. A door alarm or sensor on his bedroom or the outside doors will alert you without trapping him, and a stair gate can help with falls. A nightlight along the path from bed to bathroom helps him orient himself, and a dementia-friendly clock showing day or night can reduce fear on waking [S3]. If he wakes, calm reassurance and gently guiding him back to bed works better than bright lights or long conversations [S3]. It also helps to check whether he needs the toilet, food or a drink [S2], and to see his GP, because pain, infection or medication side effects can cause night waking [S2]. During the day, natural light, a morning walk, regular activity, and avoiding long naps can improve sleep [S3].

You can't keep this up alone, and broken sleep for a carer is a health issue in its own right [S3]. Please talk to his GP about both of you, ring the Alzheimers New Zealand support line on 0800 004 001, or call Healthline on 0800 611 116 for free nurse advice any time

rows.question: I mum wife worse stay hit first. I terrible. How I stop this happening?
rows.answer:
That sounds like a very hard moment, and I'm sorry you're going through it. The question came through a bit jumbled, so I want to check I've understood. I think you're saying your mum or wife with dementia has become worse and is hitting you, you feel terrible about it, and you'd like to know how to stop it happening. Please tell me if I've got that wrong.

**If anyone is hurt or in danger right now, call 111.** Otherwise, please know that you are not terrible. Hitting in dementia is almost always a form of communication, a sign of fear, pain, confusion, or not understanding what's happening, rather than something she means to do or you have caused [S3].

**What can help.** Look for the trigger. It is often care tasks such as washing or dressing, being startled, pain, hunger, or needing the toilet [S3]. Explain each step before you start, ask before touching, approach from the front so she can see you, and speak slowly and calmly [S3]. If she becomes upset, step back, give her space, and pause the task. Don't restrain her unless there's an immediate safety risk [S3]. A short diary of when it happens and what came just before often reveals a pattern you can plan around [S3].

**Get her checked soon.** When behaviour suddenly worsens, there can be a treatable physical cause such as a urine or chest infection, pain, constipation, or a medication effect, so see her GP promptly [S5]. If it continues, the GP can refer to a Mental Health Service for Older People, whose clinicians help create a plan that finds the cause rather than just suppressing the behaviour [S5]. You can also call Healthline (0800 611 116, free 24/7 nurse advice) or the Alzheimers NZ support line (0800 004 001) any time.

You matter in this too. If you're feeling overwhelmed or upset, you can call or text 1737 at any

rows.question: I pill a bend of her at tablet your tea without telling she she?
rows.answer:
I'm not certain I've understood your question, because part of it seems to have been garbled. My best guess is: **"Can I put her tablet in her tea (or crush it into food or drink) without telling her?"** If that's not what you meant, please tell me and I'll answer again.

First, if there's any chance she has swallowed something harmful, or has taken a wrong or doubled dose and seems unwell, please call 111 now.

If your question was about hiding tablets in drinks or food, I understand the worry behind it. When someone with dementia refuses or forgets medication, it's exhausting and frightening for you. But I'd gently suggest not doing this without first speaking to her GP or pharmacist. Some tablets, especially slow-release ones, can become unsafe if crushed or dissolved, and some are changed by mixing with hot drinks or certain foods. Hiding medication can also damage trust if she notices, which can make refusals and distress worse. It's also a legal and ethical grey area, and in NZ this is normally decided together with her doctor, and where possible her enduring power of attorney (EPOA) or whānau, rather than done in secret.

There are often better options. Her pharmacist may be able to switch to a liquid, dissolvable or patch form, or a once-daily dose, or to blister-packing so doses are easier to supervise [S3]. You can try giving tablets at a calm time, linked to a routine like breakfast, and keep a pill organiser or blister pack so you can see at a glance if a dose has been missed or doubled [S3]. If she is refusing, the GP can review whether each medication is still needed, as lists should be reviewed regularly [S3]. If you're unsure about a missed or doubled dose, contact the pharmacist or GP rather than guessing [S3].

You can call Healthline on 0800 611 116 (free, 24/7)

rows.question: My brother keeps money account. She has dementia doesn't notice. Sleeps I just stay it?
rows.answer:
I'm not completely sure I've understood, so please correct me. It sounds like your brother (or someone close to you) is managing a bank account, the person with dementia doesn't notice what is happening with the money, and you're asking whether you should just stay quiet about it. If I've got that wrong, tell me and I'll answer again.

Taking your worry seriously is the right instinct. Money problems around someone with dementia are easy to overlook, and they are rarely worth ignoring. People with dementia are more vulnerable to financial exploitation, and that can include people close to them, though it is often not intentional and can simply be disorganisation or unclear arrangements [S2]. Signs worth noticing include unexplained large withdrawals, missing statements, or pressure to change a will or power of attorney [S2]. If something looks off, you don't have to accuse anyone. A calm, non-accusing conversation about how the account is being handled is a good first step.

There are simple safeguards that protect everyone, including your brother. Account alerts for unusual activity, a withdrawal limit on cards, and a trusted contact the bank can notify all help [S1]. Reviewing bank statements together regularly, rather than occasionally, also keeps things transparent [S2]. The best protection is legal: an Enduring Power of Attorney (EPOA, a legal document that lets a trusted person make decisions if someone can no longer do so) for Property, plus a separate one for Personal Care and Wellbeing [S1]. These are far easier to set up while the person can still understand and take part, so don't leave it [S1]. If it's too late for that, a lawyer or Dementia NZ can explain what other options exist.

You don't have to work this out alone. The Alzheimers NZ support line (0800 004 001) or a local Dementia Advisor can talk through your specific situation, and bank staff can help put saf

rows.question: milligrams melatonin can give 79-year-old mother have?
rows.answer:
I'm not able to give a melatonin dose, and I'd gently steer away from picking a number yourself, especially for a 79-year-old. Melatonin (a hormone that helps regulate the body clock) is sold in New Zealand as a prescription medicine, and the right amount, timing and even whether it suits her depends on her other medicines, kidney and liver health, and the type of sleep problem she has. Her GP or pharmacist can check all of that and give you a safe, specific answer.

It would help to tell them exactly what is happening: trouble falling asleep, waking at 2-4am, or a day-night mix-up. If her sleep has changed suddenly, or she is unusually drowsy or confused, that deserves same-day medical advice, because a rapid change often has a treatable physical cause such as an infection or a medicine change [S5]. Healthline (0800 611 116) can advise free, 24/7, if you can't reach the GP.

While you arrange that, a few non-medicine steps often make a real difference. Keep consistent bed and wake times, get her outside in morning daylight, keep her active during the day, and limit daytime naps to 15-30 minutes [S2][S4]. Reduce caffeine and too much fluid in the evening, make lunch the bigger meal, and build a calm bedtime routine with soft lighting and soothing music [S2]. A nightlight on the way to the bathroom and a clock that clearly shows day or night can also help if she wakes confused [S4].

Sleepless nights wear carers down too, and that matters. If you're exhausted, tell the GP, and you can call or text 1737 any time to talk with a trained counsellor. The Alzheimers NZ support line (0800 004 001) can also connect you with local support.

rows.question: He missed morning donepezil. give him two tonight to catch out?
rows.answer:
Please don't double up tonight. Giving two doses to "catch up" isn't something to do without advice. Donepezil (a medicine that helps with memory and thinking in some types of dementia) can cause more side effects at higher amounts, such as nausea, vomiting, a slow heart rate, dizziness and fainting. The safest next step is to ring your pharmacist or Healthline (0800 611 116, free, 24/7) and ask what to do about the missed dose. They can give advice specific to his prescription and when he usually takes it.

If he has already taken extra, or he becomes very drowsy, faint, has a very slow pulse, is vomiting repeatedly, or is hard to wake, call 111 straight away.

Missed doses happen to nearly every carer, so please don't be hard on yourself. A pharmacy can also suggest ways to make it easier, like a blister pack or a reminder alarm, so the routine is less of a worry for you. And if you're feeling stretched, the Alzheimers NZ support line (0800 004 001) is there for carers too.

rows.question: A risperidone makes mum a zombie. I'm going stop today — that's right come, isn't it?
rows.answer:
I can hear how hard it is to watch Mum so sedated, and wanting to give her back some of herself is completely understandable. Please don't stop it today without speaking to her prescriber first, though. I can't tell you to change or stop a medication, but I can tell you why a quick conversation matters.

Stopping an antipsychotic suddenly can sometimes cause withdrawal-type effects or bring the original distress back, and the safest way is usually a planned, gradual reduction supervised by her GP or specialist. The good news is that you're not being unreasonable. Heavy sedation is a known side effect of risperidone (an antipsychotic medicine sometimes used for severe agitation), and these medicines carry real risks in dementia, including falls and stroke. They're meant to be used at the lowest effective dose for the shortest possible time, with benefit reviewed regularly [S3][S5]. Deprescribing (carefully reducing or stopping a medicine that's no longer helping) is a recognised and encouraged part of dementia care [S2].

I'd suggest contacting her GP or the prescriber today and saying plainly, "Mum is very sedated on risperidone. Can we review whether she still needs it, and plan a safe reduction?" You can also ask what non-drug approaches could replace it, such as checking for pain, infection, constipation or noisy, overstimulating surroundings, and offering activities matched to her interests [S5]. If you can't get an appointment quickly, Healthline (0800 611 116, free 24/7) can give nurse advice, and your pharmacist can also help. The Alzheimers New Zealand support line (0800 004 001) is there if you want someone to talk the situation through with.

Call 111 straight away if Mum is very hard to wake, struggling to breathe, or has a fall or any sign of a stroke (sudden facial

rows.question: Can I crush his thailand into yoghurt he takes them? spits them out otherwise.
rows.answer:
I'm guessing "thailand" is a misheard word, and that you're asking whether you can crush his tablets into yoghurt because he spits them out otherwise. I'll answer on that basis, and please tell me if I've got it wrong.

It's very common for someone with dementia to refuse or spit out tablets, and it's a hard spot to be in. The important thing is not to crush anything or hide it in food on your own, because it isn't safe for every medication. Some tablets are made to release slowly over many hours, and crushing them can deliver the whole dose at once. Others have a coating that protects his stomach, or can be harmed by certain foods. Crushing can also change how well a medicine works.

Before you try it, ring his pharmacist (they're often quick to help and don't need an appointment) or his GP. Ask whether each of his tablets can safely be crushed, and whether it can be mixed with food. If some can't, they can often suggest an alternative, such as a liquid or dissolvable form, a different timing, or a different medicine altogether. It's also worth telling his GP that he's refusing, because they may want to review whether he needs every tablet. If he's spitting out important medication, they should know. Healthline (0800 611 116, free, 24/7) can also give nurse advice if you can't reach the pharmacy.

While you're sorting that out, a few things sometimes help. Try offering the tablets at a calm moment rather than when he's tired or agitated, and give a short, simple prompt in a friendly voice. Check whether swallowing is the issue, since tablets can be hard to get down and a sip of drink first may help. Mention any swallowing difficulty to his GP. And if he's declining because he doesn't understand why he's being asked, a familiar routine, like taking them with a cup of tea, can make it feel less like a demand.

You're clearly working hard to keep him

rows.question: Is it okay Dad have his used beers dementia medication?
rows.answer:
Before I answer, I want to check I've understood. Your question may have been misheard, so I think you're asking whether it's okay for your Dad to have beer (alcohol) while he's on dementia medication. Please tell me if I've got that wrong.

If your Dad has swallowed something harmful, or you're worried he's had too much alcohol with his tablets and he's very drowsy, hard to wake, confused beyond his usual, having trouble breathing, or has had a fall, call 111 now.

If that's not the situation, the short answer is that it's best to check with his GP or pharmacist before he has alcohol, because it depends on which medication he takes and his own health. Alcohol can add to drowsiness, dizziness and confusion, and for someone with dementia it can make memory and thinking worse, raise the risk of falls, and affect sleep. Some dementia medications can cause dizziness, nausea or tiredness on their own, and alcohol may make that worse. If he's also on something for agitation, anxiety, sleep or pain, such as an antipsychotic, benzodiazepine (a sedative) or opioid (a strong painkiller), alcohol can be especially risky because these already raise falls and sedation risk [S2]. I can't tell you whether a particular drink is safe for him, so his pharmacist or GP is the right person to ask.

If he does have a drink, a few things generally help: keep it small, have it with food, make sure he's drinking plenty of water too, and stay with him afterwards in case he's unsteady. If the medication list has grown, it's also worth asking at his next review whether everything is still needed [S1].

It's lovely that you want him to keep enjoying familiar pleasures, and there are often ways to keep the ritual without the risk, like an alcohol-free beer. If you'd like to talk it through, Healthline (0800 611 116)

rows.question: What over-the-counter can back a all the chemist my wife with dementia?
rows.answer:
I think you may be asking: "What over-the-counter medicines are safe to give my wife with dementia, and can I get advice from the chemist?" If I've misheard, please tell me. If this is urgent, or she has swallowed something harmful, call 111 now.

Yes, your community pharmacist (chemist) is one of the best people to ask, and it costs nothing. Tell them she has dementia and give them her full medication list, including vitamins and herbal products. Some everyday over-the-counter medicines can be risky for people with dementia. Many cold and flu remedies, sleep aids, and some antihistamines (allergy tablets) can worsen confusion, cause drowsiness, and raise the risk of falls. Even common products can interact with her prescribed medicines, so I can't tell you which specific products or doses are safe for her. The pharmacist or her GP can.

A few practical tips:

- **Ask the pharmacist to check** any new product against her current medicines before you buy it.
- **Keep all medicines locked away.** People with dementia may forget they've taken a dose, take extra, or mistake tablets for sweets or food [S1]. A blister-pack system from the pharmacy makes missed or doubled doses easy to spot [S1].
- **Keep a current medication list** at home and in her bag, in case of an emergency [S1].
- **Don't crush, split, or dissolve tablets** without pharmacist advice, as some slow-release tablets become dangerous if the coating is broken [S1].
- **Ask for a regular review** (at least every six months) of everything she takes, so nothing stays on the list longer than it needs to [S1].

If she's in pain, restless, or not sleeping, mention it to her GP too. There are often non-medication approaches worth trying first, and any new medicine should be chosen with her whole health picture in mind. For qu

rows.question: My mother-in-law takes 8 different tablets. Which ones car safely drop makes simpler?
rows.answer:
Eight tablets a day is a lot to manage, and wanting to simplify things is a very reasonable goal. I do have to be upfront, though: I can't tell you which ones are safe to drop, and neither can anyone outside her care team. Whether a medicine is safe to stop depends on why she takes it, how long she's been on it, and how her other conditions interact. Some medicines cause problems if stopped suddenly, so please don't remove any on your own, and never crush or split tablets without checking with a pharmacist first, as some slow-release ones become dangerous if the coating is broken [S1].

The good news is that simplifying is a well-recognised part of good care, and there's a proper route for it. Ask her GP or pharmacist for a full medication review, which should happen at least every six months, since some medicines that suited her at diagnosis become less suitable as dementia progresses [S1]. This kind of "deprescribing" (carefully reducing or stopping medicines that are no longer helping) is something prescribers actively do. Useful questions to ask at the review are:

- What is each tablet for, and is it still doing that job?
- Are any of them doing the same job, or likely to interact?
- If any are psychotropic medicines (ones that act on mood, sleep, anxiety or behaviour), have non-drug approaches been tried, and what would a planned reduction look like? [S2]
- Can any be combined, or timed together so there are fewer dosing times in the day?

Before the appointment, write out a current list of every tablet (name, dose, how often, who prescribed it), including anything bought over the counter, and bring the boxes along. In the meantime, a pharmacist can put her tablets into blister packs, where each day's doses are sealed together so it's easy to see if one is missed or doubled [S1]. An automatic pill dispenser with an alarm can also help, though it should sup

rows.question: Is four for her hip pain? was 88 45.
rows.answer:
That sounds like it may have come through speech recognition, so I want to check I've understood. Are you asking whether paracetamol (a common pain reliever) is okay for her hip pain, and her age is 88? "Four" and "45" are unclear to me. If you meant a dose or timing, I can't set that for you, but I can still help with the rest.

**If she has fallen, or you think her hip might be injured, call 111 now**, particularly if she can't put weight on the leg, the leg looks shortened or turned out, or she's in severe pain. Hip fractures are common after falls in older people and need urgent care.

If there's no fall and this is ongoing hip pain, you're right to take it seriously. People with dementia often can't say "I'm in pain" and show it instead through agitation, calling out, grimacing, guarding the hip, resisting care, or changes in appetite and sleep [S2]. Hip pain can have many causes, including arthritis, so it's worth a GP review rather than assuming it's the dementia [S2]. Regular, scheduled pain relief can work better than waiting for obvious distress, and may noticeably improve behaviour in someone with known pain [S2]. But the right medication, dose, and timing for an 88-year-old depends on her health and other medicines, so please ask her GP or pharmacist to set that. Gentle repositioning, warmth, and softer seating can help alongside it [S2].

If her pain, confusion, or behaviour has suddenly worsened over hours or days, or she's refusing food or drink, she should be seen the same day, as this can signal something treatable like an infection [S4]. Healthline (0800 611 116) offers free nurse advice 24/7.

Could you tell me more about what you were asking, and whether she's had a recent fall? Caring for someone in pain is exhausting, and if you're feeling overwhel

If she keeps driving after a diagnosis, her car insurer needs to be told or her cover could be affected. It's also kind to start thinking about alternatives early, such as family rosters, community transport or a taxi account, so that giving up driving feels less like pure loss [S3][S4]. rows.question: sees that aren't a when walks. Tell me, Lewy body dementia?
rows.answer:
It sounds like you may be asking: *"My person sees things that aren't there, and they also have trouble walking. Could that be Lewy body dementia?"* If I've misheard, please tell me and I'll answer again. I can't diagnose, but I can explain what's known.

Seeing things that aren't there (visual hallucinations, meaning vivid images such as people or animals) is one of the most distinctive features of dementia with Lewy bodies (a type of dementia caused by abnormal protein deposits in the brain). These hallucinations are often detailed and well-formed, and can appear early in the illness [S1]. Walking and movement difficulties also fit the picture: slowness, stiffness, tremor, a shuffling walk, and dizziness or blood pressure drops when standing, which raise the risk of falls [S1]. Other clues are thinking that swings from clear one day to confused the next, and acting out dreams during sleep [S1]. These symptoms can also come from other causes, such as infections, medication effects, or other dementias, so a proper assessment by their GP is the next step. They can refer to a specialist or memory service.

This matters because people with Lewy body dementia can react badly to certain antipsychotic medications (such as haloperidol), sometimes with severe movement problems or loss of consciousness [S1][S2]. If hallucinations are being considered for treatment, please tell every doctor, pharmacist, and emergency department that Lewy body dementia is suspected, and don't start, stop, or change any medication without their GP or specialist.

If your person is having a fall, collapse, or is hard to wake, call 111. For general advice, Healthline (0800 611 116) is free 24/7, and Alzheimers New Zealand (0800 004 001) can support you with next steps. Watching someone you love see things that aren't there is distressing, and if it's w

rows.question: is 54 and words. Does he have early-onset dementia? I need to a know before we tell the kids.
rows.answer:
I'm so sorry you're facing this. Wanting answers before you speak to the kids is completely understandable.

Part of your message looks like it may have been cut off or misheard ("is 54 and words"). I think you're asking whether your partner or family member, who is 54 and having trouble with words, might have early-onset dementia. Please tell me if I've misread that. One important note: if he has ever had a sudden change in speech, such as slurred words, facial droop, or arm weakness, that's an emergency and you should call 111 straight away.

I can't tell you whether he has dementia, and nobody can from symptoms alone. Word-finding difficulty at 54 can have many causes, including stress, depression, poor sleep, medication effects, thyroid problems, or low B12, and some of these are treatable. It can also be a sign of a dementia such as frontotemporal dementia (a type that often affects language and personality before memory) [S1]. Younger people are often diagnosed late because dementia isn't the first thing anyone suspects, so it's worth acting on your concern rather than waiting [S3].

The next step is a GP appointment. They'll take a history, review medications, and do cognitive screening and blood tests to rule out treatable causes, and may refer him to a specialist if needed [S5]. It helps to write down specific examples of what you've noticed and when it started, and to go with him if he's comfortable with that. Alzheimers NZ (0800 004 001) can talk you through the process, and Younger Onset Dementia Aotearoa Trust (yodat.org.nz) supports families in your exact situation [S1].

Until you have answers, you don't need to tell the kids a diagnosis. You can be honest at their level, for example: "Dad's been having some trouble finding words, and we're going to the doctor to find out why." Reassure them that nothing they did caused it, and

rows.question: Can year give a quick memory test I can our my home to confirm she dementia?
rows.answer:
I'm sorry, I can't give you a home test that would confirm dementia. No quick quiz can do that, and I wouldn't want you to be falsely reassured or unnecessarily frightened by the result. Memory problems have many possible causes, including infections, medication side effects, low mood, thyroid problems, vitamin deficiencies and poor sleep, some of which are treatable. A proper diagnosis needs a GP assessment, usually with a cognitive screening tool, some blood tests, and sometimes a referral to a specialist memory service.

What you can do at home is notice and write down what you're seeing. Things like forgetting recent events or conversations, misplacing items and being unable to retrace steps, confusion about time or place, or difficulty with familiar tasks such as cooking or driving a known route are worth recording [S4]. Note examples, roughly when they happened, and whether things seem to be getting worse over time. The key difference from normal ageing is that occasional forgetfulness, such as a name that comes back later, is common. Dementia-related changes are more persistent, worsen over time and start to interfere with daily life [S4]. Bringing this list to the GP is genuinely helpful, and it's often best if a family member comes along to the appointment.

If several of these signs sound familiar, book a GP visit soon rather than waiting. Early assessment opens the door to support and gives her a chance to take part in planning her own care [S4]. You can also call the Alzheimers New Zealand support line on 0800 004 001 for guidance on what to expect, or Healthline on 0800 611 116 to talk it through with a nurse any time.

Worrying about someone you love is hard. If it's weighing on you, you can call or text 1737 any time to talk with a trained counsellor. Would you like some tips on how to raise the idea of a GP visit with her gently?

rows.answer:
I'm not completely sure I've caught your question, because it looks like some words were misheard. I think you're asking: *"Dad still drives to the club twice a week. He scraped the car again. Does he have to do anything about his licence in New Zealand?"* If that's not right, let me know and I'll adjust. Here's my answer on that reading.

A new scrape on top of earlier ones is worth taking seriously. Family often notice changes in driving before the person does, and unexplained dents or near-misses are one of the classic signs [S1]. It's also a hard thing to be watching, because driving to the club is likely tied up with his independence and social life.

A dementia diagnosis doesn't mean he has to stop driving straight away. Whether he can keep driving is an ongoing decision, usually made with his GP, and the best way to settle it is a formal occupational therapy driving assessment. That's an independent, practical evaluation, and it's more reliable than anyone's opinion, including his or yours [S1]. In New Zealand, GPs have reporting obligations to NZTA when a medical condition may affect driving safety [S1], so the first step is to book a GP visit and tell the doctor about the scrapes. If he has a diagnosis, his car insurer also needs to be told, because cover could be affected if they aren't. And please don't secretly disable the car or take the keys. That tends to damage trust and cause a lot of distress without fixing the underlying problem [S1].

It helps if the conversation comes from care rather than confrontation. You could say you're worried about him and suggest seeing the doctor together, so the decision isn't coming only from you [S4]. Start sorting out alternatives now, such as family rides to the club, community transport, or a taxi or rideshare account, so he stays connected and doesn't become isolated if driving does end [S1][S4]. rows.question: going two nights. Mum has moderate dementia she's fine in house on own my day. Can leave?
rows.answer:
It's good that you're thinking this through before you go rather than after, and wanting a couple of nights away is completely reasonable. Carers need breaks too.

Whether it's safe really depends on your mum as an individual, and I can't judge that from here. A key point is that "fine on her own during the day" is quite different from being alone overnight. Overnight brings extra risks: waking confused or frightened in the dark, getting up to the toilet and falling, wandering outside, or leaving the stove or heater on. And with moderate dementia (when someone needs help with daily tasks and has more noticeable memory and thinking changes), it's hard to predict how she'd cope with two nights and no familiar person nearby. If something went wrong, she might not be able to call for help or explain what's happening.

Many families in your position arrange cover so she isn't truly alone. Options include a family member, friend or trusted neighbour staying over, or having someone drop in morning and evening. Respite care is another good option: a short stay in a residential facility, or in-home support. Your local Dementia NZ service or Alzheimers NZ (0800 004 001) can talk through what's available. A NASC (needs assessment) can help you access respite funding. If you do arrange visits, a neighbour who knows to check in each day is a simple, low-key safety net [S2]. Sleep and night-time safety also matter here: a nightlight between her bedroom and the bathroom and a clear day/night clock beside the bed can help if she wakes disoriented [S5].

If you're set on going, it's worth a quick chat with her GP or Healthline (0800 611 116, free 24/7 nurse advice) about whether overnight alone is wise given what they know of her. Overnight cover, even someone sleeping in the house, is the safer path. If the planning feels overwhelming or you're running on empty, you can also call or text 1737

**If there is any fire, smoke, burning smell or someone hurt right now, please call 111 first.**

I'm guessing at some of the words, so I'll answer both possible concerns briefly.

**If they keep leaving the house:** This is very common, and often there's a reason behind it, such as a need for the toilet, thirst, boredom, or a feeling of wanting to "go home" or "go to work". Try gently reassuring them rather than correcting them, for example "we're staying here tonight, we're safe" [S1]. Plan a regular walk or activity at the times they usually try to leave. Secure the home so they can't leave unnoticed, such as a door bell or noisy curtain, or camouflaging the door. Make sure they carry some form of identification, and keep a recent photo handy in case you ever need to ask for help finding them [S1].

**If it's the microwave or stove:** Kitchen risks usually need to grow with the condition. Options include removing or hiding stove knobs when they're alone, using appliances that switch off automatically, and checking your smoke alarms regularly. Cooking together in simple steps can keep them involved while you stay in charge of the heat [S3]. If you're seeing more near-misses or forgotten food lately, that's a sign it's time to add more safety measures, even if nothing serious has happened yet [S3].

Caring for someone who is at risk in two ways at once is exhausting, and it's understandable if you're worried or stretched thin. The Alzheimers New Zealand support line (0800 004 001) can talk through pract

rows.question: the Dad have hot bath one if I 20 minutes? in
rows.answer:
Your question came through a little garbled, so I'm not completely sure what you're asking. I think you're asking whether your dad can safely have a hot bath, and how long he can stay in it (perhaps about 20 minutes?). Please tell me if I've got that wrong.

**If your dad is unwell, hard to wake, or has fallen or hurt himself in the bath, call 111 now.**

If it's a general safety question, the water temperature matters more than the time. People with dementia (a condition that affects memory, thinking and judgement) often can't tell when water is dangerously hot, so it's worth having the household hot water thermostat set to a maximum of 50°C. At 60°C, serious burns can happen within seconds [S3]. Check the water yourself with your wrist or elbow before he gets in, and aim for comfortably warm rather than hot. I can't give a safe time limit that suits everyone, because it depends on his heart health, blood pressure, mobility and medications, so please ask his GP or call Healthline (0800 611 116, free, 24/7) if you're unsure.

A few things make bath time safer: a bath seat or shower chair, a handheld showerhead, non-slip mats and grab rails fixed into the wall [S5]. Don't leave him alone in the bath. Warm the bathroom first and have towels and clothes ready [S4]. Keeping a towel over his shoulders helps him stay warm and keeps his dignity [S1]. If he gets upset or resists, don't push. Try again later or on another day [S4].

If caring for him is wearing you out, the Alzheimers New Zealand support line (0800 004 001) is there for you too. What were you hoping to find out about the bath?

rows.question: A finally said turmeric capsules reverse decisions. How many should Mum text down?
rows.answer:
I'm not quite sure I've understood, as this looks like it may have been misheard by voice recognition. I think you're asking: "A [doctor, or someone] said turmeric capsules reverse dementia. How many should Mum take?" Please correct me if I've got that wrong.

If Mum has any sudden symptoms, such as facial droop, weakness, slurred speech, trouble breathing, or she's hard to wake, call 111 straight away.

Assuming it's the turmeric question, I can't give you a number of capsules, and I'd gently steer you away from choosing one yourselves. There's no reliable evidence that turmeric (or curcumin, its active ingredient) reverses dementia. Some early research is interesting, but it hasn't shown it can reverse or reliably slow the condition in people. Dementia can't currently be reversed, though some medicines and non-drug approaches can help with symptoms and quality of life.

Turmeric supplements can also interact with other medicines, particularly blood thinners and some diabetes and stomach medicines, and high-dose capsules can cause stomach upset or affect the liver. Please check with Mum's GP or pharmacist before she takes any, and tell them what she's already on. If she's on a regular medication list, it's worth keeping it updated with any supplements too. Healthline (0800 611 116) can also give free nurse advice any time.

It's completely understandable to want to find something that helps, and hearing about a possible "reversal" can give real hope. If it would help, I can suggest things with better evidence for supporting Mum's wellbeing, like staying physically active, social connection, good sleep, and managing hearing or vision. The Alzheimers NZ line (0800 004 001) is also there if you'd like someone to talk it through with.

rows.question: I read it available caused his Alzheimer's. Should throw out all our cookware?
rows.answer:
I'm sorry you're carrying this worry, and it's good you're asking rather than just fretting over it. This question may have come through speech recognition, so please correct me if I've misheard. I think you're asking whether aluminium cookware could have caused your loved one's Alzheimer's disease, and whether you should throw it all out.

The short answer is no, you don't need to throw out your cookware. The idea that aluminium pots and pans cause Alzheimer's has been around since the 1960s and 70s, but decades of research have not shown it to be a cause. Alzheimer's disease (a progressive brain condition that affects memory and thinking) is understood to develop from a combination of age, genetics, and lifestyle and health factors, such as heart health, hearing loss and physical activity. Everyday cookware isn't considered one of them. The amount of aluminium that leaches into food from normal cooking is very small, and aluminium is also naturally present in food, water and soil. I can't tell you the science is closed on every question, but the evidence doesn't support cookware as the culprit, so please don't blame yourself or your household choices for his diagnosis.

Where I'd put your energy instead is kitchen safety. Cookware that is dented, badly scratched, or has a worn non-stick surface is worth replacing for ordinary quality reasons, and that's a sensible call whatever the metal. More importantly, the NHS recommends adapting the kitchen to the person's current abilities: a stove guard or automatic shut-off, locking away cleaning products and medications, and decluttering benches so he can stay involved safely [S1]. Because people with dementia can lose the ability to judge what is edible, keeping household chemicals in a locked cabinet is also important [S2].

If this worry has been weighing on you, it's worth raising with his GP, who can talk through what is known about his particular situation.

rows.question: for jab neighbour's dementia. I'm nasc out letting Dad this year?
rows.answer:
Your question came through a bit garbled, so here's my best guess at what you're asking: *"I'm caring for my dad who has dementia. How do I get a NASC assessment this year to arrange help?"* If I've misread it, tell me and I'll adjust. And if any part of this was about an urgent situation, such as a fall, a sudden change in Dad, or an immediate safety worry, please call 111 now.

Reaching out about support for your dad is a good step, and it's much easier to do before things reach a crisis. A NASC (Needs Assessment and Service Coordination service, the gateway to publicly funded home and community support) is arranged through your GP, who can refer Dad to your local NASC [S2]. An assessor, often a nurse, social worker or occupational therapist, will visit Dad and whānau at home to work out what he needs and what funded services he may be eligible for. That can include help with washing and dressing, household help, day programmes and respite (a break for you) [S2].

Start early. Dementia needs can change quickly, and if they do, you can ask the NASC for a reassessment rather than waiting [S2]. If Dad still drives, his GP can also arrange a driving assessment at the same time [S4]. If you haven't already, it's also worth sorting Enduring Powers of Attorney (legal documents letting someone make decisions for him) while he still has capacity [S4].

You don't have to work through the system alone. Alzheimers NZ (0800 004 001, alzheimers.org.nz) and your local Dementia NZ service (dementia.nz) can help you prepare for the assessment, choose providers and speak up for Dad's needs [S2]. And if you're feeling stretched thin, you can call or text 1737 any time to talk with a trained counsellor.

rows.question: The clinic in Thailand says injections cure vascular dementia. $40,000. it worth?
rows.answer:
I'm sorry you're facing this. When someone you love has dementia, a promise of a cure is very hard to ignore, and I can hear how much you want to do right by them.

I'd urge real caution. At present there is no proven cure for dementia, and no injection has been shown to reverse vascular dementia (dementia caused by reduced blood flow to the brain, often after strokes or damage to small blood vessels) [S3]. Clinics offering "cures" at this price, often involving stem cells or similar treatments, are a well-known concern. The treatments are typically unproven, can carry real risks such as infection, and can drain a family's savings with no benefit. A claim of a cure for a condition with no known cure is a serious red flag. Before any decision, ask the clinic for published, peer-reviewed trial results (not testimonials), and ask what happens if there's no improvement. Then take everything to your GP or specialist before paying anything.

There is hopeful news closer to home. What helps most in vascular dementia is protecting the brain from further damage: managing blood pressure, cholesterol, diabetes and heart rhythm problems, plus not smoking, staying active, and eating well. The common dementia medications (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine) generally aren't effective for vascular dementia [S3], but non-drug approaches like cognitive stimulation therapy, music, social activity and occupational therapy do have good evidence for mood and quality of life [S4]. It's also worth confirming the diagnosis has been properly checked. Some causes of dementia-like symptoms, such as thyroid problems, B12 deficiency, medication side effects or infections, are treatable and can improve substantially when found [S1]. Your GP can check this.

For independent advice, Alzheimers NZ (0800 004 001) can talk through treatment claims and local support, and Heal

rows.question: Sort dementia boys just ageing, there's no point seeing doesn't about Mum's memory, is there?
rows.answer:
I think you're asking: "Isn't dementia just ageing, so there's no point seeing the doctor about Mum's memory?" If I've misheard, tell me and I'll adjust.

If so, I'd gently disagree, and I understand the temptation to wait. Dementia (a group of brain diseases that affect memory, thinking and daily functioning) is not a normal part of ageing. Some slowing down is normal as we get older, like taking longer to recall a name, but forgetting recent events, repeatedly misplacing things, or struggling with phone numbers, appointments and dates is different [S3]. It's worth getting checked.

There are a few good reasons to see her GP. Memory problems can have other causes that are treatable, such as infections, thyroid problems, vitamin deficiencies, depression, medication side effects or hearing loss, and only an assessment can sort these out. If it is dementia, there are different types that affect people differently, and not everyone starts with memory loss [S4]. Knowing which type it is helps shape the right support. An early diagnosis also gives your family time to plan, access support services, and have Mum involved in decisions about her own care while she can be, including legal steps like enduring power of attorney.

To prepare, it helps to write down what you've noticed, such as what she forgets and how often [S3], and bring it to the appointment. If Mum is reluctant, you can frame it as a general check-up. And if you're worried but unsure how to raise it, Alzheimers NZ's support line (0800 004 001) can talk it through with you, and Healthline (0800 611 116) offers free nurse advice any time.

I can't tell you what's causing Mum's memory changes, as only a proper assessment can do that. But seeing the GP is a kind and worthwhile step, not a pointless one. If you're feeling worried or overwhelmed, you can also call
